speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NIGERIA-ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN DIPLOMATIC MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon.
members will recall that last July I said that the Canadian government intended to establish diplomatic representation in Nigeria as soon as circumstances permitted. We were subsequently informed that both the United Kingdom and Nigerian governments welcomed this decision. I now wish to inform the house that it is planned to open a new mission in Lagos in April of this year. Mr. Thomas L. Carter has been appointed head of the mission and, for the period up to the independence of Nigeria, he will have the title of commissioner for Canada.
Mr. Carter has served in several diplomatic posts abroad including a two year term as charge d'affaires in Warsaw. In 1957-58 he was the Canadian member of the international commission for supervision and control in Viet Nam. Last year he attended the imperial defence college in London. Mr. Carter served for five years in world war II with the Royal Canadian Artillery, and was awarded the Military Cross while with the 2nd field regiment of the 1st Canadian division in Italy.
With its some 35 million inhabitants, Nigeria will be the most populous state in Africa. It is a country with considerable potential for development, and is expected to play an important role in African affairs. As this development takes place there will undoubtedly be an opportunity for expanded trade with Canada, and for that reason I am glad that the Department of Trade and Commerce is appointing an officer to the new mission. Nigerian officials have already visited Canada from time to time in the course of preparing themselves for the new responsibilities they will take up on attaining independence. We have been pleased to give them some help, and we hope to be able to do more in the future through our technical assistance program. These associations augur well for a fruitful and cordial collaboration directly between Canada and Nigeria, as well as through our relationship within the commonwealth.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is a very happy omen that just before I read this statement I received the following dispatch directed to our Prime Minister from the Prime Minister of Nigeria:
My dear Prime Minister, I was delighted to receive your message telling me that you had selected Mr. Carter to be the Canadian commissioner in Nigeria. I look forward to welcoming him in April and I assure you that we are all very happy that this positive step has been taken to demonstrate Canadian good will toward our country.

subtopic: NIGERIA-ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN DIPLOMATIC MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by the minister will be welcomed, of course, by those of us who sit in this group, as I am sure it is welcomed by all members of this house. One wonders why the minister has taken this particular occasion to make an announcement of this kind. However, since he has done so, we welcome it not only for the reason that it is important to establish a mission in this particular front of the commonwealth as such, but it is also a means of promoting the desired unity among commonwealth nations as an instrument for peace in the world at this time.
I wonder if the minister could now announce to the house, as he has made the announcement of this particular mission, whether the government has yet reached a decision about the appointment of an ambassador to Mexico. The vacancy there, I think, is almost a year old, and in view of the importance of that country and that mission to Canada perhaps the minister would take advantage of this opportunity to tell us what are the government's intentions in that regard.
The minister might also tell us why Mr. Carter is to be called a commissioner and not, as his associates in other commonwealth countries are called, high commissioner.

I noticed in the statement of the minister that providing diplomatic recognition and representation would likely lead to an increase in trade between our two countries.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Emilien Morissette for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Some hon. members may recall that last year I brought up the issue of higher pay for members of parliament, and at that time I promised that I would put down a resolution drawing attention to this matter. I have not done so, and I thought I might take this opportunity to explain the reason.
Since I spoke last year the matter has certainly been complicated in my mind. It has not been so much a question of second thoughts, but I can see that there are more nuances about this than I thought at the time. I can only say that I hope to bring up this question again on another occasion when hon. members are at liberty to express grievances. I am glad to note that one or two other members, for example the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) and the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) have indicated that they are taking an interest in the matter.
Since I originally brought this up, I have found that a large section of the public does not think we are worth even what we are getting. I never mind getting bitter letters, but I am very much surprised at the generally accepted view across the country that we are not worth all we are getting at the present time.
The second thing I have discovered, after considering the membership of this house, is
[Mr. Dlefenbaker.l

that there are many more men of comparative wealth and substance than I had imagined; and while there may be urgency in some sections for more remuneration it is quite obvious that the same is not true for many of our number. No doubt this complicates the issue, but maybe if we have a debate on this subject later it would be interesting to hear from such hon. members.
Another matter which has been troubling me with regard to any move toward higher pay is this. I have come to believe that if we do get more pay we are going to require a greater diligence in attendance and this, of course, raises all kinds of problems to which I certainly have no immediate answers.
The last point which has bothered me since I brought up the matter was perhaps best expressed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) last year, when he indicated that politics for most hon. members should be a semi-professional occupation; that full time politics in the main was for a few professional politicians, but that for the generality of members of parliament it should be a part time occupation. This view, which seems to be held by most of the-let us say-more experienced members, especially in the older parties, is not one that I agree with, but it is certainly one which is going to need some shaking down.
I repeat that I will attempt to bring up this matter on a later occasion, and I trust that some of those members who are interested in it will take the opportunity to indicate their views in the house. As I say, I discovered that while many people who follow our proceedings feel that perhaps we should be getting more, there is a very strong feeling abroad in the country-it does not scare me too much-that we are not worth what we are getting now.
There has been some unrest and dissatisfaction among some hon. members about this particular debate. This found expression yesterday in the speech of the hon. member for Calgary South, and there has been some very pointed comment in the press about the performance earlier on of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in particular. I think there must be some general agreement among us that since the attendance during this debate is relatively low-and we have no committees functioning at the present time-in the main this debate is neither interesting nor edifying nor amusing to most of us.
It certainly seems to be a pity that there should be a blight put so early on the high spirits in which most hon. members gather at the beginning of a session. I certainly am not speaking for our group-if I can use that

term, since it seems to have been appropriated by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin)-but I do feel we should look very seriously at the way our debates are going, and the fact that obviously we do not like to listen to each other, in the main. I for one would hesitate to establish a standard for our performance, but I should like to say that if we all spoke with the fine diction, modulation and pleasant voice of the seconder, the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), this unrest might not be so apparent. I have heard it said that Mr. Solon Low, the former leader in this house of the Social Credit party, used to practice his speeches beforehand by speaking into a whirring air-conditioning fan, and that the former member of parliament, Mr. John Blackmore, used to prepare for house performances by practicing yoga.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How do you prepare?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I welcome that interjection from the hon. member from Brome-Missisquoi because I have heard that he prepared for his contribution to the throne speech debate by declaiming in the echo chamber of room 16 just across the hall. One account that reached me said this practice was interspersed with "pause here for applause". I can only hope that such assiduity and confidence is appreciated in his constituency.
The next topic with which I wish to deal is one to which reference has already been made, the performance of the Prime Minister. The subject of power and those who hold it has always fascinated me. The people who wield power is for me the most fascinating aspect of human society. In Canada the epitome of power rests with the Prime Minister. He is the actual head of our state. Whoever he may be, and whatever his party, he is the exemplar, one might say the standard of political action to the nation. In the light of this I wonder how much thought the Prime Minister has given to the nature of his performance, not so much as the decision-maker but as the glass of political fashion, the mold of political form.
More particularly we have had the emergence through reiteration in an uncharacteristically blunt form by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) of the charge that the Prime Minister is unnaturally concerned with an evangelistical type of politicking that is undignified and very much a sham, related to the slick, lowest common denominator approach of the huckster. And we all know who the huckster is supposed to be. I believe I can give some of the phrases used in the address of the Leader of the Opposition in this debate:
The Address-Mr. Fisher
-confused by evangelistic inefficiency which amounts very often to ineptness-demagogy for democracy and propaganda for performance. Procrastination, political manoeuvring, drift-
Perhaps we should thank the Leader of the Opposition for this head-on summation. I was here on January 20, 1958, for the Prime Minister's greatest forensic triumph. I can recall it best, as perhaps others can, with the words spoken the next day by Mr. Colin Cameron, the former member for Nanaimo, who said:
It was a rather tragic scene we witnessed yesterday. We saw something else that was not very pretty to behold. We saw a magnificent hatchet job done on the Liberal opposition in this house and, as one who on occasion can use a fairly sharp machete myself, I give the Prime Minister full marks for a magnificent hatchet job.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order. The hon. member knows it is contrary to the practice of the house to read from newspapers or outside documents which reflect upon the conduct of members in the house.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a quotation from Hansard of January 21, 1958.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: It cannot be approved if it is a quotation from Hansard which appeared in a newspaper.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, this is a quotation from a speech made by the then hon. member for Nanaimo when he was a member of this house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I beg your pardon. I thought the hon. gentleman was quoting from a newspaper.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Nanaimo went on to say:
And yet I wonder if that is the role which a prime minister of Canada should play. I wonder if he should have rushed with such relish into the abattoir-When I saw him bring whole batteries of guided missiles of vitriol and invective in order to shoot one forlorn sitting duck-a sitting duck, indeed, already crippled with a self-inflicted wound -I wonder if the Prime Minister believes in the humane slaughter of animals.
Well, that slaughter by the Prime Minister led directly to the dissolution of parliament and the subsequent arrival here of Tories, 200 and more in strength. The scope and exhilaration of the victory made the January 20 performance-the wagging finger, the ironic pauses, the piercing "why did they hide it"; "why didn't they do it"-a political pivot of our times. But here we are, three sessions later. The government and the Prime Minister should have their second wind now, but it is still the old wind we hear soughing; attack, attack, attack interminably, with many blusters of quotations and counter-quotations.
Perhaps others get a different opinion of the political interest of the people. Frankly I

The Address-Mr. Fisher cannot find a ripple of interest in 1957 or 1958 and its events. The Liberals are gone, and except amongst a few civil servants at Ottawa there is little nostalgia for them. The interest is in this government. Where is it going? What are its ideas? What bold measures is the Prime Minister taking with this almost embarrassing mandate behind him?
Malcolm Muggeridge observed recently about Aneuran Bevan that he is the only politician of his acquaintance who is not still a boy. When I watched the Prime Minister at the sixth or seventh repetition of his January 20, 1958 performance, given here last week, I thought that are we indeed not boys to get excited or exasperated by such attacks.
Frankly, I had great hopes that the Prime Minister was not a genuine Conservative, that the approbation of bank presidents or the opinion of Bay street would mean much less to him than the little people, his fellow Canadians as he is wont to call them; that here was possibly a sort of prairie Lincoln. I can only comment that his attempt to seek a repetition of the triumph of that earlier January appeals much less than repeated hearings of the Gettysburg address.
We are in mid-term of this government, and it is almost indistinguishable in performance and leadership from the low key last years of the Liberals. What is there arrestingly new about any of its legislative acts? Most of them have been merely extensions of existing Liberal legislation. Aside, perhaps, from the creation of the new department of forestry is there anything which enables us to say "This is where a Diefenbaker government is different"? We have had, of course, the emergence of a counterpart to Mr. C. D. Howe in the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).
I am probably one of the few opposition members who feel there is a lot of talent and ability on the government benches, but that all too little of it is on the treasury benches. One looks them up and down. Where are the men of brilliance who should cluster in some radiance around the Prime Minister? All I can see twinkling is the Minister of Finance; and unfortunately to me his is the kind of twinkle that is orthodox and conventional, not what many hoped from Diefen-bakerism.
I have been much in Ottawa during the off-session, and I know how true it is that we have never had a cabinet that meets so much. One tries to imagine the subjects of these deliberations. Discussion can be valuable, and long discussion should precede decisions, bold decisions. But neither in

legislative programs nor in public statements by the cabinet ministers do we get an over-all picture of where all this discussion has led. We had a vision of the northland far as human eye can see, but we have little of the detail along the way. And' as an aside, Mr. Speaker, I have been surprised at the antagonism in the government ranks to the one visionary we seem to have in the cabinet, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton).
But when one judges from the statements of the farm groups which I have read, or the general forecast for agriculture, one is not really clear as to what is this over-all policy. In this very debate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) spends his time, in the fashion of the Prime Minister, in proving that the Leader of the Opposition is a fool on this particular topic. This to me is not the enunciation of any clear-cut, over-all policy.
When I think of defence I would be willing to bet that this government has pondered more on this particular topic and on the monetary situation than any other government in Canadian history. I can imagine all the weary hours they have wrestled with the submissions of all the highly technical experts, but to what avail in coming up with a policy that is immediately understandable? I noticed that one of the men in the press gallery commented the other day that members of parliament do not know much about defence policy. I will admit I do not know much about defence policy, but I am not getting it and I do not think any other members of parliament are getting it from defence policy statements released by this government or the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes). This, of course, is perhaps a problem of communication; it is not coming out.
I perhaps have been a dreamer all the way along to have expected to understand the policy of the government. I know one veteran pundit of the Ottawa scene told me rather jadedly last week that there really is not any choice any more for Canadian politicians; that they are in a grey world riding on circumstances and reined in by the experts. Another professor of my acquaintance put it more bluntly. He told me, "You want to get all this out of your mind that you are important, that you politicians are important any more. You are circumscribed in Canada by the voice of the experts, by the strictures of the international situation. You are frozen almost to inanition by the contending pressures of national groups or the regional pressures within our plural society".

I refuse to believe, Mr. Speaker, that we as politicians should be so deflated and so given to a grey world, so given to compromise. I still like to hope and feel that from the radicalism-I can only look to the Prime Minister-that I am sure he has, we are going to get something at least in the field of education. This is something that concerns a great many people in Canada; and they will no longer accept the excuse in English speaking Canada, or they will not accept it much longer, that because of the French Canadian position we cannot have leadership in the field by the federal government. It comes down to this. We all want equality of opportunity for our children right across the nation wherever they come from, and we all want a good standard of education right across the country. As I look back, all I can say is that there has been great disappointment. I recall the fine remarks that were made on this subject by the late Hon. Sydney Smith when he first came into politics. But what have we had in the field of education? Nothing. We have had a few commonwealth scholarships, a sort of playing around the fringe of the problem.
In housing we are in this situation. For the middle income groups there is no longer the housing shortage there was, but we are still not getting anywhere in housing for the lower income groups. There is no great progress in transportation. We have a near chaos. You have the farmer against labour, against the railways, against the truckers in one round circle. You have another royal commission, and it is just an interim one. You have regulations abounding, hearings interminable, labour negotiations a repeated marathon; subsidy here, there and everywhere, and the whole picture so complex that hardly anyone comprehends the whole. Last year we voted $20 million to take care of an immediate crisis for the railways; and almost mocking ourselves, we pumped this $20 million through a complicated freight rate structure in order not to disturb the complex balances and pressures that we have within the freight rate structure and the transportation picture. To my mind the whole situation in transportation today is a travesty of either competitive enterprise or bright, consistent regulation. All we have is an interim royal commission.
The anomalies of government action in the transport field point less to the dilemma than to the confusion of an apparent free enterprise ethic in the government. We have been under the impression that some members of the cabinet are partial toward free enterprise. I can think of no better example than the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees)
The Address-Mr. Fisher for whom it is claimed that he has put T.C.A. in its place and has brought C.P.A. into the field. What do we get in the brief from the air industries and transport association of Canada, which was put on our desks the other day, a group of free enterprise entrepreneurs? What are they asking for? They want the government back into the regulatory field. They concluded:
It is our further opinion that the unrestricted issue of licences cannot be construed as being in the best interests of the public, either from a convenience or a necessity point of view.
This is what we find repeatedly with the free enterprisers. The point I bring out here is that enlightened public interest should be the guiding principle, and this government ought not to take action because of some free enterprise myth. Look at this example of the Minister of Transport, the great free enterpriser. What is he doing about pilotage? I wonder whether hon. members are aware that this free enterpriser added a number of civil servants to the payroll in order to provide pilotage service that is demanded by the Shipping Federation of Canada, a group of foreign shippers. Therefore we now have pilot boats, we have pilots on the government payroll, put there by this pressure from free enterprise. That is an inconsistency, a mockery. Today we have a report from Washington that negotiations seem to be completely disrupted in trying to get along with the Americans on pilotage. One of the ironies there is that those Americans who are looking after their pilotage rules and regulations do definitely believe in free enterprise. They cannot understand this free enterprise government of ours being willing to go along with more civil servants on the payroll.
My opinion is that this government service is fine; perhaps it is right, but I just want you to note the inconsistency. If we go on kidding ourselves that there is real competition, any more, or a real free market economy in the larger sense, I think we are wrong. The whole tendency of capital accumulation today is toward mammoth size or bigness; a duplication of government-like bureaucracy in business; and thus there is cut out this whole matter of competition that we have been used to in connection with the free enterprise myth. It seems to me that this is one of the arguments which we should not bother with any more, but what we want to consider is enlightened public interest and what assistance and leadership the government should give. We are operating under a chaotic set of regulations in so many parts of the economy.
I was interested to note that the Prime Minister wants a committee on scrutiny such

The Address-Mr. Fisher as they have in the British parliament. I do not know how much he has gone into the details of this committee, but it is one that goes into such organizations that are equivalent to our crown corporations. It is a small committee which operates without any publicity; in effect you might say it operates in camera. It keeps going over all kinds of complicated legislation to see that there is nothing that will impinge upon individual freedom and also impinge upon other authorities. I think myself it is a good idea, but it will have to be thought our very carefully. I did some work on committees which sat during the past session and I have done some reading, and I came to the conclusion that the enthusiasm the Prime Minister has for committees is all very well but I do not think he has thought out some of the fine points of where we should go with the committee system.
We have a committee on public accounts with an opposition chairman. This is supposed to be based on the British model. The British committee does not work as ours does. It is a small committee of only 35 members. It breaks down into groups of seven. Those groups take certain areas. They work in between sessions; they go to the site of things; they examine things closely. They are a working committee which is to check things carefully. Partisanship does not come into it; it is not that kind of a committee, and it is not the kind of committee that we have in this House of Commons. Therefore to talk about the British model and not do anything about creating something similar is just not fair.
One of the other things I noticed in all the comments of the Prime Minister on committees has been that he always says we must not have anything that is too much like the United States example, because the United States committees infringe so much upon the executive. All I can say is that, despite the McCarthy hearings and despite some of the other hearings of United States committees, if you examine what they do you cannot help but be impressed with how they get down to things and the information they turn up.
One of the decisions we have to make in regard to committees, if we are going to go further with them, concerns this mysterious boundary line between policy and administration. I know I was on a committee last year on mines, forests and waters, and I know that committee wandered far from the administrative level into the area of setting the policy the government should follow. I am not frightened of that aspect. However, if we are going to have more committees we


want to have very clearly in our minds what they are going to do, what their powers are going to be.
This may sound presumptuous to some of you, but upon investigation I found that no one had written anything on Canadian committees, aside from a very short dissertation in Mr. Dawson's "The Government of Canada". I tried, in an article that is published in the Waterloo Review, to bring some of this information together. I suggest that some hon. members might be interested in it, in that it does comment on the committees of last year.
Before I leave this point I should like to say that one of the problems I found in checking the attendance records of the committees was that on only one committee last year did the French speaking members of this house have a fairly high attendance record. I know the attendance record is not something that is completely valid, because members come in and members go out. However, if you look at that attendance record you will note what little part in our committees was played by the French Canadian members, except on one committee in which they happened to do some speaking in their own language. One of the difficulties is that if you have committee working in two languages it is going to break down or drag out. Certainly, so far as committee work is concerned, if we are going to take committees seriously then we have to do something about getting our French Canadian members working on them.
One of the other things I discovered as a result of checking the attendance in committees and the number of people who spoke is in connection with the argument that was put up a number of times in this house by the Liberals that they just did not have time to take part in committee work because of house activities. This argument is not valid. The busiest Liberal on the committees last year was also the busiest one in the house, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). One other point I discovered in my checking was that the people who took the most part in the committees, that is private members, were also the ones who took the most part in the house.
If we are to improve attendance at committees, which ranges between 40 per cent and 50 per cent during their sittings, it seems to me there is no use in passing rules and regulations. We have to have leadership from the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in making sure that their members take committee work seriously. This is the point I wanted to place before

the Prime Minister in connection with this tendency toward saying that committees will do the job. They will only do the job if the members of your party are convinced that committee work is really important.
Here you will only get important work done if these members are briefed and have some kind of continuing facilities within the committees. It is almost ridiculous to put the average Canadian M.P. in a committee up against some of the specialists whom he confronts. He has not any advice; he has not any counsel, except what he can gather up by himself. This is matching David and Goliath, and David has not got a slingshot. It seems to me that one of the ways to make what I consider a fairly decadent parliamentary system work is to do more with the committees. Until we consider the points I have mentioned, I do not think the committee system is going to be as useful as some people believe.
I did want to touch in this debate on something that is, I suppose, considered by some to be a matter of importance; that is the position of socialism. At least some of us within the C.C.F. have believed we were socialists, I think most of us. I want to refer to the position of socialism with reference to what is being heralded as the new labour party.
There is one point I wanted to make at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, and that is many people are saying that organized labour has no business in politics; that it is an economic organization and as an economic organization should not get into politics. This, to me, is not a principle at all, it is an argument of expediency. It may have something of value in it, but it is not a question of principle. We have very few principles in politics other than the normal ones that we properly get from our religious heritage such as truth, justice, morality and matters like that.
Whether or not organized labour should get into politics is a different question. I am much more interested in whether organized labour, once it gets into politics, will do something to liven up the Canadian political scene. There is one point here, and my explanation may seem obscure to some of you, but one of the things that bothers me about the political scene in Canada is that the two areas in which we have the best educated people with the widest administrative experience are the civil service and the large corporations, the organizations that have knit the industrial and retail pattern of our country.
The Address-Mr. Fisher
The civil service is automatically ruled out from taking any part in politics, which is probably just as well. In so far as corporations in Canada today are concerned, I may say that the last year I worked at Queen's university there were some 27 very able boys in the graduating commerce class, but not one of them was going into business on his own. They were all going into the large corporations. The people in those corporations do not go into politics. They are forbidden; it is an unwritten law. These corporations are the part of our economy that tends to be in a power struggle with labour, and when labour goes into politics in an organized fashion one of the good things that will come out of it will be the fact these corporations will be shaken out of their indifference to the political scene. I suppose most members get as fed up as I do with the standard assumption by some of these people in business and industry that politicians are a bunch of dodos, and that they are too good for politics. I think organized labour coming into politics may change that situation a little, and there may be a greater interest on the part of people who tend to be labour's economic rivals.
Another of the difficulties of labour in politics is that they will tend to bring into politics-this is disturbing a good many people in the C.C.F.-the jurisdictional disputes. This will be difficult without doubt. Perhaps the crucial point bothering me about the new party is, is labour a genuinely radical movement? Are they not one of the groups that are now against reform and change? In other words, are they dragging their feet holding on? I have tended to wonder about this. All I can say is that I now feel, from the people who have the idea of the party-I do not argue that this has gone down to the grass roots yet-that they are convinced that organized labour in politics is going to be a radical force, a socialistic force if you want to put it that way. I am not one of those who thinks socialism is a dirty word.
In my opinion, those who decry labour in politics are missing the point. It is the right of every one of us in any group or association to take a political interest, so long as we do it on the understanding that our government is going to be carried on by evolution and not by revolution. I do not believe anybody in Canada is worried about the labour movement in Canada being revolutionary. The question that is in the minds of many of the people throughout our particular party who are going to be working in this is whether the evolutionary idea will be dynamic enough.
All I want to say here-because this may be carried beyond this particular forum-is that I and many others with whom I have

The Address-Mr. Fisher worked in the C.C.F. party will not have much time tor a new party that is stand-pat, that is not socialistic in its direction.
One of the reasons labour has thought of getting into politics and has gone as far as it has gone is dissatisfaction with the two old parties. I am not one of those socialists who feel that power is all important. I think influence is as important. If the emergence on the scene of this threat does one thing- shakes up political ideas-I shall be happy. If you look at the new party in terms of the financial strength and the organizational skill it is going to have, what you will find is this. We may not have people like Mr. Grosart, but there is a real organization and there is the promise or prospect of real financial strength behind this party.
For my part, if either the Liberal party or the Conservative party tends to answer this challenge, which is a demand for some distinctive party of reform in Canadian politics, I shall be quite happy. I should be happy to see the hon. member for Essex East rise in his place and really lay down the proposition that the Liberal party is one of the left, a party of reform, a genuine party of Liberalism.

It is going to be a long and tough fight, but it is going to be tougher if the Liberal party or the Conservative party begin to act and move like genuine reform parties. But if they do not do so I think it will get on the move and go much faster. I am a history teacher, and when I say "go faster" I have in mind a fairly long period of time; I would say within a decade or 15 years. I think it will be tragic, of course, in some ways to those of us who are interested in history, to see the departure of one old party, perhaps the one that was launched by Sir Francis Hincks or perhaps the one that was launched by George Brown, but I think it is something that may very well come. To those of you who think labour has no business in politics I should like to put this question. Who has not today any business in politics?
I started off by remarking on the reaction I had found amongst many people to the effect that politicians are not worthy of the salt they now get. Unless you get more people taking part in politics, then you are going to find this cynicism about it. If there are members of the house who feel that I am far too jaundiced in my view of what people think of politicians, I should like to have that

view corrected. I should like to hear some chapter and verse that convinces me that we really have the status we think we have when we perform in this house.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise this morning, to take part in the debate, my mind naturally goes back to a year ago, when on January 15, 1959, I had the privilege and pleasure to be introduced to the house.
First of all, I would like to say how much I was impressed, during the last session, by the splendid and masterly way in which you guided the discussions of this house.
We were therefore pleased when, at the start of the session, we found you again at your post after your long period of travel across the world. We are now assured that our discussions this year will again be marked by dignity, and even good-fellowship, as you will be there to guide them with efficiency and impartiality, and I wouldi even say, with your usual sense of humour.
This year, Mr. Speaker, you will be seconded by a colleague of mine who is one of the most brilliant barristers of Quebec. The choice you have made of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn), as deputy chairman of this house could not have been more fortunate.
My ties of friendship with the hon. member for Quebec South, go back 30 years or

so, when we were at college together. I had the opportunity of observing him in the exercise of his profession in Quebec, and I may assure you that the House of Commons will greatly benefit from his experience as a lawyer and as a politician.
As it is only proper, I also would like to congratulate the new Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), who after having played a very significant part as Deputy Speaker, has now brought his experience and his fine personality to the federal cabinet.
The new minister is the son of a great lawyer of rare distinction. He will certainly continue to bear proudly on the political scene a name which, about 15 years ago, he covered with courage and glory on the battlefields of Normandy during the dismal, gory hours of the last war.
I have much the same feeling with regard to the new Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker). May I be allowed to congratulate him too on the great ease with which he expressed himself in our own language. The hon. minister enjoys, without any doubt, the esteem of all members of the house, as well as an unquestioned prestige in every province and throughout Canada.
And now, what about my good friend the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) who a few days ago, gave us his views, those of a specialist, on the economic situation in Canada.
I believe, and I told him so, that he would have made an excellent lawyer, for many reasons, not the least of which is certainly the fact that the hon. member for Rimouski knows how to select his cases. He pleaded a great cause, and did so with elegance and much success.

Before I tackle my main theme, Mr. Speaker, allow me to recall painful and sad events, as my colleagues from Quebec have done before me.
The Address-Mr. Fortin
Without any partisanship-if I have any such-I would like to say a few words, with all the objectivity of which I am able, about the disquieting events which happened in my province last fall.
You will recall that, on September 7, a Quebec premier, the Hon. Maurice Duplessis, died in the sparsely settled northern area which he had largely helped open up to civilization.
His province had found to replace him a great and gallant soldier. It had found a public man of great integrity, a brilliant lawyer and an excellent orator.
Immediately, the Hon. Paul Sauve set to work. He worked for the sole purpose of carrying on a task which had forcibly been abandoned, but he was imbued with great patriotism, one which, I would say, was both provincial and national. Unfortunately, death, whose sinister activity never abates, picked him as a second victim.
The province of Quebec and the country as a whole will no doubt remember that great Canadian who, in the troubled hours of the last war, did not hesitate to leave his seat in the Quebec legislature to fight in Normandy at the head of the gallant soldiers of the Fusiliers Mont-Royal.
Mr. Speaker, I represent a constituency which last year was suddenly, and for no valid reason, left to fend for itself. Just after the general elections in March 1958, in which the voters of Montmagny-L'Islet reelected their former member after he had promised to put forth his best efforts on their behalf during his term of office, he dropped them without prior consultation. Perhaps this was unfortunate, but it had a happy result, because it gave the people of Montmagny-L'Islet an opportunity to recover and to show their confidence in the Conservative government, a confidence which they would again display if the opportunity arose.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, my constituency is located 35 miles east of Quebec city, on the left bank of the St. Lawrence, that is to say on the southern shore. On the north, it is bounded by the St. Lawrence, on the east, by the constituency of Kamouraska, on the south by the United States, and on the west by the constituency of Bellechasse.
From the standpoint of economy, the constituency may be divided in two sections. First there is the industrial section, which includes the city of Montmagny and the smaller but thriving town of L'lsletville. There is a spirit of friendly competition between the two. Two well known foundries are established there. There are also factories turning out furniture and metal goods. It can

The Address-Mr. Fortin be said, Mr. Speaker, that the city of Mont-magny is among the most prosperous and progressive in Canada. Thanks to its industries, it is self-sufficient.
The remainder of the constituency, of course, is essentially agricultural. However, I should like to mention the fact that there is, in Montmagny-L'Islet, a delightful spot located on the banks of the St. Lawrence river. I refer to the lovely village of St. Jean Port-Joli.
This community is famous for its craftsmen. There are about a hundred of them engaged in wood carving and ceramics. The better to identify this little village for the information of those who are familiar with that part of the country, may I just mention, for instance, the masterpieces of wood carving turned out by the Bourgault brothers.
They had the honour of carving a bas-relief panel that was presented to Her Royal Highness, Princess Margaret. They also made one for the former governor general of Canada, the Right Hon. Mr. Massey and, if my memory serves me well, I think that among the distinguished citizens who received some of their work I might mention the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).
I wish-and this is a recommendation I am making-that the Canada Council would assist those craftsmen who, apart from pursuing their art for their own personnal profit, operate a school of wood carving where, each year, quite a few pupils acquire a basic knowledge of that art. There are also in the constituency of Montmagny-L'Islet two islands. One of them, Crane island (lie aux Grues) is also the site of a small rural parish. It seems that the citizens of that parish have preserved more than others the customs and traditions of the past. I am pleased to point out-which is all to their credit-that even in their speech they have something that we lack. They have preserved old expressions dating back to the beginning of the colony, and their very accent singles them out as islanders although they live only three miles away from the coast.
There is also a second island, Grosse Isle, now administered by the federal Department of Agriculture where a pathology laboratory is located.
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with other parts of my remarks, may I call it one o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned I noticed that I had made an omission which I would like to correct at once. I realized that I had unwittingly omitted to tender my congratulations to the new parliamentary secretaries. Though coming a bit late, my tribute is none the less sincere. I also would like to express my best wishes to our two new colleagues, the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb), and the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif), to whom I wish a lot of courage and patience, because I feel he will greatly need them.
Before bringing my audience back to Ottawa, I would like to recall in this house the memory of a great citizen who was a credit to the political world of his country in the last century. I refer to a citizen of Montmagny whose name you cannot fail to remember, I mean Sir Etienne Pascal Tache. Tache was born in Montmagny. His family was of rather modest means, though it is reported that before the war, or rather, before the battle on the plains of Abraham, the Tache family was considered very well-to-do. He practised medicine in the constituency of Montmagny-L'Islet for several years. When the war of 1812 broke out, young Tache spontaneously and voluntarily offered his

services. He was no doubt inspired by his patriotism, and perhaps also by the spirit of adventure, being a direct descendant of the great discoverer of the Mississippi, Louis Joliet.
During his first years of medical practice, Sir Etienne Pascal Tache remained in the background. He devoted himself to his fellow-citizens. He applied all his sympathy and knowledge to the healing art. But one day, however, this devotion became a burden. His fellow-citizens pressed him to go into politics, and it is thus that he was elected member for the constituency of L'Islet in the legislative assembly.
After filling several positions in the country's government, Sir Etienne Pascal Tache became prime minister of Canada. Before confederation he was twice prime minister. He was also chairman of the famous and historical Quebec conference which laid the foundations of Canada's constitution. Tache was a great patriot. He was also a great soldier. He served as aide-de-camp to Her Majesty Queen Victoria who, at one point, decided to call this outstanding Canadian citizen to Windsor castle to make him a knight. Later he was given the title of Sir Etienne Pascal Tache.
Soldier, physician, statesman, knight, prime minister and a father of confederation, Tache was above all a great Christian, of the type you still find among our people.
Even on his deathbed, Sir Etienne Pascal Tache appeared to have forgotten all the glory he had reaped throughout his political career, and he made this confidence to a close friend who was at his bedside: A man does not have to be a prime minister, nor to reap his share of human glory; the one important thing is to be a good Christian and an honest man.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have discharged a duty which I consider sacred, by lifting the veil of Canadian history and reviving the memory of Sir Etienne Pascal Tache, a great Canadian who was particularly gifted as far as intellect is concerned, but more so with regard to character, a quality which is as precious as it is rare and only belongs to those who know how to dedicate themselves. May I be allowed to say, in closing this part of my remarks, that it is the intention of the people in my riding to erect this year, a monument to the memory of Sir Etienne Pascal Tache. A subscription has been launched among the people, and we hope
The Address-Mr. Fortin to be able to proceed with a demonstration of national scope, because, in my constituency, we consider Sir Etienne Pascal Tache as a local son, though it should be kept in mind that he was, first of all, a great Canadian personality.
Mr. Speaker, last November I had the privilege of attending the parliamentary conference of NATO in Washington. Before going there I also had the advantage of taking part in an organized tour in the United States which enabled us to learn something about American military organization. We toured all the main military facilities on United States territory. There were delegates from every member nation of NATO. My companions were the hon. members for Algoma West (Mr. Nixon) and Vancouver South (Mr. Broome).
First of all, we were able to visit Fort Bragg in North Carolina, Mr. Speaker, which is the centre of the airborne regiment of the American air force. Thanks to a very careful schedule, we were shown all phases of the training of American paratroopers, from the moment where the young man arrives at the base to the minute he makes his first parachute jump. We also had the privilege to attend the launching of a rocket, of the type called "Honest John".
From Fort Bragg we went to Norfolk, Virginia, which Americans pronounce "Nor-fik". There we had the opportunity to attend extremely interesting lectures by admirals of the American, British and French navies. We also had the privilege to see and visit the magnificent American aircraft carrier Randolph and the whole naval base.
From Norfolk we went to visit the Marine Corps training camp where, by means of graphs and most interesting talks, we were given a demonstration of a marine corps landing. We also saw the military camp for American troops at Fort Eustis and, lastly, we went to Fort Langley, Virginia, where we were able to visit the air base.
At Fort Langley our attention was held by something very special, because we had the great privilege to attend a conference given by American scientists specializing in space research. We were privileged to see that famous capsule which some day, we trust, will carry a human being in space, and some of the delegates even sat in it, not without first expressing the hope it would not be fired just then.
From Fort Langley, we crossed the United States to go to Colorado Springs to visit the

The Address-Mr. Fortin NORAD organization. There we visited the control room and witnessed a very interesting demonstration. But I believe that, at Colorado Springs, what was for us, Canadian delegates, the most important and interesting feature was the astonishment of our European colleagues who were literally astounded by the spirit of co-operation which exists between Americans and Canadians.
When we met General Kuter and Air Marshal Slemon, we had the opportunity of exchanging a few words about Canadian sovereignty in the field of defence, in relation to NORAD.
On that point, Air Marshal Slemon said, in the presence of the hon. member for Algoma West, that the American commander, who has to be absent from the base about two thirds of the time, was automatically replaced by the Canadian commander, Air Marshal Slemon. That goes to show that, most of the time, American troops under NORAD come under the complete and absolute command of the Canadian commander. Furthermore, after having explained to us what was going on, Air Marshal Slemon asked me to convey to my Canadian fellow citizens a message which I consider of great importance. We often hear it said in Canada, he remarked, that when Canada joined NORAD for the defence of the North Atlantic, our country sacrificed a part of its sovereignty. Now, here is what Air Marshal Slemon said in this regard: "No one sacrificed its sovereignty in adhering to NORAD, but if someone had sacrificed it it would certainly not have been Canada, but rather the United States, because most of the time it is I, a member of the Royal Canadian Air Force, who am in command here.
From Colorado Springs, we went to Omaha, Nebraska-and that was the last leg of our trip-where we visited Strategic Air Command, called SAC. We saw the underground control and we had a demonstration of the communications which operate twenty four hours a day between the strategic centre of defence, at Omaha, and different areas of the globe. A demonstration was given us by General Power himself, which allowed us to note that in ten to fifteen seconds General Power was able to communicate with all bases, either American or NATO, spread around the world, with Turkey, Italy, Portugal and France.
I should like to express my gratitude to those who enabled me to make this rewarding
[Mr. Fortin.1
and instructive trip. Allow me to express a wish that was also voiced by the NORAD authorities in Colorado Springs. I wish that other members were given the opportunity- and I must call this an opportunity-of visiting the NORAD organization in Colorado Springs, so that they might be more familiar with the situation. Then, being better acquainted with the policy agreed on, we could together discuss these matters in public or in the house.
Mr. Speaker, it is with great interest that I listened to the speech delivered here a few days ago by my good friend the member for Hull (Mr. Caron). I listened to him and I even read his speech afterwards, because we know that the editor of debates makes certain corrections at times so that speeches are more easily understood when they are read than when they are heard.
It was quite amusing to hear the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) say that he was scandalized because a great number of Conservative members took part in the election campaign in Russell constituency.
He particularly took to task the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon); however he did not mention any other member of this house, but said that there were many. By inference, we can deduce that if the member for Hull can say that there were many Conservative members in Russell constituency, he must have been there himself.
Then how could that right, which the member for Hull claimed for himself, of campaigning in Russell constituency be denied to other members? Perhaps, you will say, there was the question of distance, since he lives so close. And I admit that this is a point in his favour.
But just the same there is one thing which I want to draw to his attention. Let me remind him of the days that he spent in Mont-magny-L'Islet constituency last September. I had no objection whatsoever because I got the impression that, following every meeting addressed in Montmagny-L'Islet by the member for Hull, my position was improving.
In this case, though, he should agree that he was far from home. I see him looking at me and smiling. He smiles more readily now than he did at that time. But he was not the only one.
Before criticizing people who participate in an electoral campaign, one must have a

clear conscience. And I find satisfaction in reminding him of this saying:
People who live in glass houses should not throw stones.
In Montmagny-L'Islet an army was routed. I think of my friends, the members for Megantic (Mr. Roberge), for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) and especially the member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) driving his Cadillac around along the border doing all he could to reverse the verdict.
There were a good dozen of them. But that is not all. We even saw, at one time, the member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). He was given the opportunity to learn a lot about the province of Quebec. At the last moment, the Liberals realized that the situation was almost desperate. No doubt you will understand, Mr. Speaker, for you are from Quebec. Well, they even brought in the former minister of veterans affairs, the Hon. Hugues Lapointe, and that settled the question once and for all.
One thing struck me also in the speeches delivered by my friends and more particularly by my friend the member for Hull. I wish I could quote his own words in their entirety, but at one point he talked about horses. Here is what he said, Mr. Speaker: I am not an expert on horses, but when it comes to election horses I know what I am talking about.
I pondered these words and tried to make out what the member for Hull had in mind, which is no easy task. It is just like trying to make one's way in a virgin forest. You have to push branches aside to make headway and recognize the situation.
However, coming back to the horses of the member for Hull, I wondered, when he mentioned a political horse, whether he was referring to the horses which, under the former Liberal administration, used to be on the payroll at Petawawa.
In any event from the way he talked of horses, I thought he might have had some experience as a horse-trader. With his permission, I should like to make a suggestion. Perhaps the hon. member might go to Quebec and try to sell the provincial Liberal party a better horse than they have now.

In the speeches we have heard from the Liberal group, great stress has been laid on the so-called emptiness of the speech from the throne.
The Address-Mr. Fortin
One thing that struck me is that the first Liberal members who spoke said there was nothing in the speech from the throne.
Surely, you heard them mention that. Then they read the speech again, and they did find something. Some people are slower learners than others. Well, they finally realized that there was something in the speech from the throne.
I should like to point out a few of the things contained in that speech.
The first point was to the effect that the government continues to regard as a primary goal the achievement of the greatest possible measure of controlled disarmament.
Now this opens the door to a debate on international and military matters as well. My hon. friend the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) has dealt with this at some length, so there is little need for me to stress it. However, perhaps I might say-and this is a personal view, and I hope no one will come back tomorrow and say it was the opinion of other people I know-I think this matter of disarmament should be considered with the utmost care.
I remember and could hardly ever forget that ever-famous statement made by Mr. Manuelsky, one of the first graduates of the Lenin school in Moscow. Speaking to the Americans, he said: "We are not yet ready to fight you. We need thirty years, and when we are ready, we will launch a great peace offensive."
I think they are pretty well on schedule at this time. Since 1931, which means 29 years ago, we all know how the U.S.S.R. has been concentrating on rearmament.
Do they now feel they are in a position to destroy the world? It is not for me to say. However, they had in fact planned 30 years ago that when they were ready they would launch a great peace offensive. Well, what is the nature of this peace offensive?
First, there is the matter of uncontrolled disarmament, and second, this new form of war known as economic warfare.
Therefore, without going further into this matter, I will say that the question of disarmament is an extremely topical question, and a very touchy one. However, I am fully confident that the leaders of the NATO countries will exercise control over the field of disarmament.
In the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, mention is made of economic and technical
446	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fortin assistance to underdeveloped countries. I think this matter may be related to my earlier remarks to the effect that if today Russia considers it necessary to assist underdeveloped countries, it is certainly not for humanitarian reasons, but as a means of spreading its disastrous influence.
We are obviously living in an era of uncertainty. Can we truly say today that we are in danger of war?
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the apprehension of war, felt by nations in the past, no longer exists.
In the past, when a country thought of declaring war, it was most of the time with the assurance of winning that war. The victim of such an aggression also felt sure of destroying the aggressor.
This is not the case now and nuclear war means world destruction. Russia knows it as well as NATO countries. This is why they now resort to a new policy. The economic war.
After a close study of the speech from the throne, I note that mention is made of a project of lesser concern perhaps to easterners but surely of interest to westerners and that is the development of the Columbia river. The Liberals are greatly concerned with the economic situation. Let me tell them that they will have ample time to discuss this matter.
They said they wanted to discuss at once the unemployment problem which is mentioned in the speech from the throne. We hear talk about seasonal unemployment, and just plain unemployment. Here again, they will be given the opportunity of studying these conditions.
The speech from the throne mentions the revision of the Civil Service Act.
There is talk of establishing a new department of forests, forests being the wealth of our country. A Department of Forests will be created to develop them, to stimulate research in the field of forestry and thus automatically improve this country's economy as a whole.
There was also some mention of housing assistance and, quite recently, it was announced that the federal government intended to raise from 4 to 6 billion dollars the loans guaranteed by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and from 1 to 1J billion dollars the loans to be granted by that organization.


Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that this legislation will certainly help procure jobs for our workers and, in consequence, contribute to the welfare of our Canadian people.
At any rate, I shall close my remarks by saying that even if the speech from the throne does not mention in detail each and every piece of legislation which the government proposes to introduce, it was worked out so as to allow all possible discussion.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to mention the proposal which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) recently made with regard to the repatriation of the Canadian constitution. It is needless to say that in this matter I share the views of my good friend, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau). All Canadians favour the bringing home of the constitution and, as the time I have at my disposal prevents me from elaborating on this point, I shall just say that the remarks of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue are very much in accordance with my way of thinking.
Mr. Speaker, if ever a commission is set up-as I wholeheartedly wish it will be- in order to proceed with the entire revision of the Canadian constitution, I would like, as the Prime Minister pointed out, the articles 91,	92 and 93 of the British
North America Act to remain unaffected. Besides I would even go further than the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue on a particular point, and ask that the scope of section 133 be extended.
In the field of bilingualism, we have today, so to speak, the bare essentials. We want more than that, and I am pleased to tell the hon. member for Hull-which will make him realize that when I spoke to him a moment ago I was sincere-that the little inquiry he is conducting at present has its good side. We are entitled, in view of the country's development and the good will of the various departmental heads, to demand total bilingualism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the assertions of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, the traditional speech from the throne is more noticeable this year for what it leaves out than for what it reveals about government policy or about important legislation to be introduced.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to congratulate the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) who moved the address in

reply to the speech from the throne. I congratulate him first because it was a personal honour for him, and also for his constituents.
I also congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) who brilliantly described the political situation as she sees it. Unless I am mistaken, I think this is the third time that a member of the three united constituencies of Stormont, Dun-das and Glengarry either moves or seconds the address in reply to the speech from the throne in this house. I think the fact that she was chosen bodes well for her future.
To you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, I renew the congratulations I extended to you a few days ago, and I add my very best wishes.
Mr. Speaker, this government refuses to solve the grave problems facing Canada, and in many cases even denies their existence.
Tight money, housing, high interest rates, unemployment, the unfavourable trade balance are all problems which are being left unsolved.
The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) had an opportunity, while he held the floor for 40 minutes, to give us his views on those important matters which concern the Canadian nation. He also had an opportunity, in the time at his disposal, to tell the Canadian people and the house what action his government is contemplating to deal with the problems I have mentioned. He preferred to deal with other matters. That is his problem, Mr. Speaker, but I say that the financial and monetary policy of this government is in a slump. And although a Conservative member said the other day that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) was hailed by the British people at Albert Hall in London -which is true-nevertheless it is as true today that London newspapers take an altogether different stand towards the present government. Indeed, one has only to read London newspapers, and many others throughout England, to see that, as far as economy is concerned, they feel the present government is a bad government. Such is the opinion of the London Economist which says that the policy of this Conservative government is a poor example of economic and monetary administration.
Tight money and high interest rates are the most important problem now facing the government. Since the Conservative party came to power, the cost of living has increased by 5 per cent; interest rates have
The Address-Mr. Chevrier reached an unprecedented level. Workers, farmers, businessmen, merchants, school boards and municipalities can borrow only at prohibitive rates.
Small merchants are now in a state of uncertainty and on the brink of bankruptcy. What has he to say now, that minister who interrupted me last year when I referred to the policy of the government towards small merchants, and who was telling me: "But what did you do yourselves?"
What is now happening to small merchants is pitiful, so much so that, as a result of credit restrictions, they are now in very serious difficulties. And to prove it, I merely have to quote an article published in La Presse of January 12, 1960, entitled:
Bankruptcy increased by nearly 50 per cent in the Quebec area. Credit restrictions and irresponsibility on the part of those concerned are to blame.
Those were the words used by Mr. Robert Cotd, protonotary of the Quebec superior court.
A little further on, he stated:
That increase of nearly 50 per cent is, first of all, the result of credit restrictions which were in force during the last twelve months.
And I go on to say that a man has to pay from 7J to 8 per cent interest to get a mortage loan.
Government bonds have decreased very much in value. In some cases, they are only worth $80. Why is this? It is because the government, having to borrow large amounts of money to make up its shortages, is causing a record inflation in this country.
Those shortages, Mr. Speaker, have reached a fantastic sum, about one billion more than under the Liberal administration. Yes, it was those same Conservatives who had promised to cut down expenses by eliminating the wastefulness and extravagance of the previous administration. They promised an increase in social security benefits. It is true that they increased those benefits by $106 million in 1957, but they made it up by increasing taxes by more than $350 million.
They had promised a new agreement with the provinces. However, last October the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), answered categorically that there would be no other formal agreements before 1962. They had promised to reduce expenses; but they increased them by one billion dollars. They had promised lower taxes but they have raised them considerably. They had promised

The Address-Mr. Chevrier to balance the budget. In 1957-1958 they had a deficit of $38 million. In 1958-1959 the deficit reached $862 million whereas in 19591960, according to the figures now available, the deficit will be about $425 million.
Moreover, the government is spending much more than it collects in revenue. It is piling deficit upon deficit, and, in order to fill the gap, it resorts to enormous loans, causing a scarcity of funds, and the tight money policy which the government says it does not favour. They have increased the national indebtedness by nearly $2 billion because of repeated borrowing. When a1 government competes with private enterprise for cash loans, money obviously becomes scarcer, and the interest rate goes up. From August 1958 to January 1960, the revenue of treasury bonds climbed from less than one per cent to more than 5 per cent. This, in a word, is tight money policy. All the while, the cost of living is rising considerably. It has now reached its highest level since the Conservatives have been in power. And to exonerate itself, the government tries to put the blame on others. That monetary policy also has an impact on unemployment. During the twelve months of 1959, unemployment figures in Canada reached an average of 350,000, a third of whom, i.e. about 130,000, being in the province of Quebec and from 50,000 to 60,000 in the city of Montreal. Conditions in the province of Quebec from an employment point of view, are worse than in any province except in the maritimes. And what is the government doing to remedy unemployment?

I mean the winter works plan. I will tell you: the winter works plan, according to which, 50 per cent of the cost of labour is paid to municipalities, resulted in the federal government paying, under that plan in 1959, $6,250,000, less than $1 million of it in the province of Quebec. And it has employed from
35.000	to 40,000 persons, 6,000 of them in the province of Quebec, which is very little when we know that there are between 135,000 and
140.000	unemployed in that province. Of what use is a winter works plan employing but 6,000 people?
Therefore, it is obvious that such a plan does not live up to the expectations of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), as he expressed them a few weeks ago, and even in October last.
I ask the house: what has become of that public works program of $1,180,000, so much advocated by the Conservatives? It simply evaporated. We do not hear anything about it any more. It evaporated just like the famous vision of the Prime Minister is now evaporating slowly but surely.
What about the statements of the Minister of Labour on the subject of unemployment?
I will recall them to the house. In 1958, the Minister of Labour said:
It is our duty to see to it that not a single Canadian should lose his job this year.
In 1959, the Minister of Labour said:
Toward the middle of 1959 we will have reached the end of our difficulties.

When there are 370,000 unemployed, are we at the end of our difficulties? The Prime Minister said, in 1959, when referring to unemployment-and listen to this, it's brilliant:
The worst is over, and we are slowly heading towards better conditions.
And it is needless to recall the famous statement made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign, when he said:
As long as I am Prime Minister, no one will suffer from unemployment in Canada.
I now pass to another point, the deficit in our external trade. The hon. member who spoke before me did not seem very concerned about this unfavourable trade balance. But just the same, it has reached a disturbing level, that is, nearly $1,200 million, which represents, Mr. Speaker, 42 per cent more than in 1958; and the economic blocs now forming in Europe are a danger for our external trade as well as for our export trade.
I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) that in my opinion measures that he seems to be taking now should have been taken three years ago, so as to get in touch with representatives of various regional blocs in Europe. It is only at the beginning of the present session that he and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) went to Paris to discuss the relations that should be established between those various groups.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that our exports have gone up slightly, but our imports have increased much faster. Our trade balance with the United States shows a deficit of 80 per cent. On the other hand, our exports to the United Kingdom have increased by only $6 million, but they have decreased not only with other Commonwealth countries but also with other world countries, except the United States.
In 1958, 58 per cent of our exports went to the United States. In 1959, this percentage was increased to 62 per cent. This goes to prove that we depend more and more on the American market. The same applies to our imports of which about 68 per cent come from the United States.
This is just what the Conservatives complained about so bitterly when they were sitting on this side of the house. They promised to straighten things out and in proof of this, the Prime Minister made his famous statement to the effect that 15 per cent of our American imports would be transferred to Great Britain.
This dangerous situation of which our opponents complained so much is only getting worse today. It is a dangerous situa-79951-0-29
The Address-Mr. Chevrier tion for the Canadian economy and it is due to the financial policy of the government, in that it has caused a scarcity of money and therefore high interest rates.
There is another conclusion to be drawn from the present situation, Mr. Speaker. It is our economic integration with the United States which would greatly endanger our economy, as does a considerable decrease of our exports to the commonwealth and European countries.
To what extent will our trade be affected by the organization of regional blocs now being formed? Will the common market and the free trade area adversely affect our export trade? And how about the Soviet union bloc? If countries of the Soviet union ever decided to enter into serious competition with us, it may well be that the European countries would be obliged to buy products and goods from those countries rather than from Canada. Such questions should be considered seriously and continually by the government, whose policy is uncertain and confused.
The common market, as I said a while ago, has been operating for three years now. How does the government plan to overcome the effects of the tariff union of the Six and of the free trade union of the Seven. Indeed, a proposal was put forward by Britain to the Minister of Finance, but we never heard about it and this house was never informed of the plan put forward. In order to stimulate trade between themselves, European countries are lowering tariff barriers while Canada is raising its own.
The Minister of Finance is sly. Mr. Bennett at least was not afraid to express his views on the question of tariff protection. He said on many occasions: I will blast my way into the market of the world. The Minister of Finance, I say it again, is sly. He gives us to understand that he will liberalize the trade market but at the same time he raises the tariff barriers. The anti-dumping legislation, the tariff increase on wool and vegetables, the Japan agreement, those are trade restrictions aimed at a greater protection.
How can we ask the European countries to adopt a freer trade policy if we increase our tariff protection? There is only one solution and it was given in this house two years ago by the Leader of the Opposition, that is, an agreement with the countries of the Atlantic community for the establishment of a free trade area between those countries and the United States and our country.
Since that proposal was put forward, many businessmen accepted it and have sponsored it throughout the United States. I feel that

The Address-Mr. Chevrier as far as we are concerned such an agreement would have the effect not only of guaranteeing the military existence of NATO but also of placing the western countries in a better position to enter into pacific coexistence with the Soviet union in the economic field. We Canadians have another reason for promoting such an agreement because it is the only real and positive way of reducing our economic dependency on the United States and of diversifying our trade while increasing it. For all of those reasons, the Canadian government should have, as early as 1957 I think, started negotiations for an agreement.
