Now, sir, if I may, with your permission I would like to pass to another matter which to me is of extreme importance and which I think is also of importance to the Canadian people. I refer to the policy, or the lack of policy, of the government in the field of international aviation. That policy, it seems to me, is not only shortsighted but is doing Canada a great deal of harm. It is doing Canada a great deal of harm because of the concessions that are being given to foreign countries, because of the exchanges in traffic rights, exchanges far in excess of what we receive, which have been made since this government have been in office.
Before the present government took office, Canada in its negotiation of bilateral air agreements with other countries held consistently to the firm position of exchanging third and fourth freedom rights; that is to say, giving the right to pick up and discharge traffic at one point in Canada in exchange for the right to Canada to pick up and discharge traffic at some suitable point in the other country. It was recognized that to go beyond that would not be in Canada's interests, and certainly not in the interests of Canadian aviation.
Since the present government has been in office it has deviated very materially from that policy. Concession after concession has been granted to foreign carriers, to the point that our own position has been endangered. In some cases the concessions have involved the granting of fifth freedom rights in exchange for rights which were not the equal of those we were giving; that is to say, we were granting rights to pick up and discharge traffic at a point in Canada to be carried onward to some other point in some other country. This policy has been detrimental to our own carriers, and has particularly hit a hard blow at Montreal as an international airport.
Mr. Speaker, these statements which I have made are broad and of a general nature, and

perhaps they will be found sweeping. But I intend to give details. I intend to give four examples of cases where the Canadian government, because of what I have said in the first place, gave away rights far greater than it received in exchange.
The first example is the granting of fifth freedom rights between Montreal and Chicago to two European air carriers. The present government has given to both France and Germany the right to pick up and discharge at Montreal traffic between Montreal and Chicago. Before these concessions were made, France and Germany had the right to carry traffic originating in their own countries to Montreal, and traffic from Montreal back to their own countries. These two countries also had the right to take traffic originating in their own countries to Chicago and back to their own countries from Chicago. However, neither of those countries had the right to pick up traffic at Montreal and carry it back to Chicago or vice versa.
Canada itself, under its bilateral air agreements with the United States, does not possess the right to fly non-stop between Montreal and Chicago. In other words the Canadian government has been entirely unsuccessful in obtaining rights from the United States for a Montreal-Chicago route. However, by the agreements it has made the present government has enabled two foreign air carriers to operate a non-stop service between Montreal and Chicago. Those two European carriers have been able to enjoy obvious rights and advantages in Canada without competition from a Canadian carrier. The loss of income, sir, in this case has been considerable.
What did we receive in exchange for these valuable concessions? We obtained from France fifth freedom rights between Paris and Rome, and from Germany fifth freedom rights between Dusseldorf and Vienna. But the obtaining of these traffic rights in Europe was only part of the operation, and it was still necessary to negotiate an air agreement with the two countries in question, namely Italy and Austria and, in order to obtain them, to grant to Italy and Austria traffic rights in exchange for what we required.
To my mind this is clearly a case of exchanging the substance for the shadow. There is no doubt that we have given in this case far more than we have received, for we have not only diverted a considerable amount of traffic from a Canadian carrier, but in the process we have also weakened our own bargaining position with the United States and have placed fresh obstacles in our path in an effort to obtain a change in the bilateral agreement with the United States so that we may ourselves operate a non-stop service between Montreal and Chicago.

There is a further disadvantage which must not be overlooked because of its dangerous implications. Permitting the two European carriers to serve Montreal and Chicago on the one flight provides them with an additional heavy traffic generating point, and consequently allows for a frequency of service through Montreal to Europe far beyond the requirements of the traffic originating at Montreal. This results in two foreign carriers obtaining at Canada's expense an undue proportion of the traffic offering at Montreal.
The second example that I want to bring to the attention of the house is the naming of Toronto as an additional point of call for the British air carrier. The naming of Toronto as an additional point at which the British carrier could pick up and discharge traffic was a very far-reaching concession; because Toronto, as the house probably knows, originates more air traffic than any other city in Canada.
There was no compensation whatsoever to Canada in exchange for this lucrative privilege. We obtained from the British government certain rights between the United Kingdom and the continent which, however, have no value unless, as in the case of Germany and France, the other countries concerned agreed to grant them, and they could be expected to do this only in exchange for the granting of further traffic rights at some point in Canada. I am not unaware that the granting of this concession to the city of Toronto might, on the face of it, appear attractive, but when one goes into it one can come to no other conclusion but that it is detrimental to Canadian aviation, that it is not in the interest of the air lines and that is is also not in the interests of their employees.
I tried to put on the record the other day a telegram which I had received from the president of local 698 of the United automobile workers. I should like to take this opportunity of doing so. It was addressed to me on November 27 following a speech on this subject which I made in Montreal, and the president, Mr. Malley, says:
Local union 698 UAW absolutely concurs with criticism Conservative air policy. Certain granting British Airlines Toronto rights will in the near future cost some members of our union their jobs through pooling forced on TCA to protect lost revenue.
I should also like to read a further telegram which he sent me on January 22 in answer to a request from myself for permission to read his telegram. It is as follows:
Reference your telegram January 22. Permission to use our telegram November 27 granted. Know for certain pooling negotiations TCA-BOAC almost 79951-0-294
The Address-Mr. Chevrier
concluded. BOAC has advised if successful all ground handling and maintenance engineering positions our members wiped out. Have learned British government contemplates major changes BOAC management due unfavourable financial position.
In an editorial which appeared in the London Daily Mail dated January 18, 1960, it is clearly set out that B.O.A.C. is in a very serious financial position-there was a £14 million deficit for 1959-and it seems to me that what is being done is tacking on to a Canadian carrier some of the financial difficulties of the British carrier,
The third example is the recent negotiation of an air agreement with Italy. The primary function of a bilateral agreement is to provide for air service between the two countries involved. This agreement is simply one-sided. The government has negotiated an agreement which does not in the usual manner provide for the exchange of traffic rights for a Canadian air line at Rome and an Italian air line at Montreal. It grants Canada the right to operate to Rome by way of Lisbon or Paris, with intermediate pickup rights at Lisbon or Paris, and to operate with the onward traffic rights from Rome to Bangkok and points beyond.
What concessions did Canada make in order to obtain from Italy the right to land at Rome passengers picked up at Lisbon or Paris and for the further right to carry traffic beyond Rome to Bangkok and other points? Canada granted to Italy the right to operate on a route from Italy to Montreal without intermediate pick-up points but with onward rights from Montreal to Mexico, Montreal to Chicago and Montreal to Los Angeles. These were three tremendous rights given in exchange for the little pick-up right we got from Lisbon, and/or Paris. Not only that, but the Canadian government gave the Italians the right to go on to Chicago, a right which no Canadian carrier itself does possess. Furthermore, that concession affects the revenue of the Canadian carrier which operates to Mexico by creating additional competition, so that the revenue position, because of these three onward rights granted to a foreign carrier, will substantially affect the position of Canadian aviation as a whole.
Finally, there was the granting of additional rights to air carriers of the United States in April, 1959. The only concession which the United States gave to Canada-and it is of doubtful value-was the one whereby the Canadian carrier was authorized to extend its Halifax-Boston service to New York. The United States, on the other hand, obtained several trans-border routes which they did not have before.
I will concede at once that one of the most difficult air agreements to negotiate is with

The Address-Mr. Chevrier the United States. They will not give an inch. Then why should we give an inch? Why, if we are unable to obtain rights we want from the United States, should we give them the advantages which they have obtained under this agreement? I have a list of them here, but unfortunately because of the lack of time I am precluded from putting them on the record.
I cannot in the time available to me deal more completely with the subject, but I do want to mention two serious difficulties. One is the establishment of the air union in Europe, a kind of common market in the air. Three of its members-Air France, Lufthansa and Air Italia-all possess these onward rights in Canada, and the position created by the establishment of the air union means that there will be a great deal of pooling by these companies which will detrimentally affect the revenue position of the Canadian carriers.
Then again there is the question of the jet age. The countries which negotiated these agreements with Canada knew full well what the jet era meant before they negotiated to obtain these rights from Canada. I say this with respect to the minister, who is in his place: that it appears to me as if in some of these cases the delegation acting on behalf of Canada was told "go over to the foreign country and come back with an agreement at any cost." It also looks as though the foreign country-the country negotiating with Canada .-knew that Canada wanted an agreement at any cost. If that is the case, I warn the government that it has a long way to go in order to recoup these concessions which it has in so many cases given away to foreign countries in exchange for rights of dubious value.
I am sure this must have been in the minds of the air industries and transport association when at their last meeting, assembled in conference at Montreal, they took a very dim view of the position in the international aviation field. In the first place, they took the minister to task for his interference with the decisions of the air transport board and condemning the policy of the government in respect to the field of aviation. Then, on Friday last, they saw the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)-and I presume the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) was there also-and submitted a brief outlining the detrimental position in which their industry had been placed.
Here may I be allowed to put on record, with respect to another class of traffic-not the international class-this sentence which is contained in that brief:
It is significant to note that commencing in 1958, jthe year that decontrol of class C came into effect,

the air industry met its first serious reversal. The real effect of this decontrol could not be evaluated until 1959 when a full year could be analysed. This analysis showed that many established operators of long years standing will not be able to break even, even before depreciation and that this is caused by loss of revenue to the new class C type operators. It is alarming to note the number of carriers who have, within recent months, gone into either voluntary or involuntary bankruptcy or else just out of business.
I thought I should deal at some length with this matter because I believe it is of extreme importance to the Canadian people who take pride in the aviation industry which has played such a tremendous part in the war and postwar periods.

Mr. Speaker, before going into the subject matter of the remarks I propose to make this afternoon, may I first according to custom, extend sincere congratulations to the young and able member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Dealing with a subject with which he is quite familiar, the economic situation, the young member for Rimouski painted a very clear picture of it.
I would add that as a result, he has disposed of many arguments put forward by some of our hon. friends opposite who dealt with Canada's economic situation.
May I also take this opportunity to congratulate the highly capable, charming and amiable representative of Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), who seconded the address. The member for Grenville-Dundas has learned from the long experience of two former members dear to her, the former member for her constituency and the present member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). With remarkable talent and assurance, she gave us a clear and precise picture of the life and problems of her constituents.
It is a great pleasure at this time to congratulate the new Deputy Speaker of the house, the highly popular member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn), who was appointed to this high office by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). Having known the member for Quebec South for many years, I have every reason to believe that he will do a fine job and show the same judgment as he has shown in many other occasions, with honour and dignity.
I have known the Deputy Speaker in other circumstances, because for several years-I

shall not say how many, as I have little desire to add to his years-he was my legal adviser when I was mayor of my municipality and reeve of my constituency. I therefore wish him every success in his new duties. When serving as legal adviser to various municipalities, he was liked of all and numbered only friends in the municipal field.
I must also say a word of the appointment of our two new colleagues in the federal cabinet, namely the Associate Minister of Defence (Mr. Sevigny) and the Minister of Public Works, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker). I wish them both every success in their new office.
During the memorable visit last autumn, of the Prime Minister and his lady in the province of Quebec, I had the pleasure and honour to accompany them for one day. The warm welcome they were tendered everywhere we went was in contrast, and still is in striking contrast, with the dim picture which hon. members of the official opposition are giving us today, when speaking of our leaders, and ourselves, that is the Conservative members.
The Prime Minister was warmly received by the people of the province of Quebec, and, the province, on the other hand, remembers this with pleasure. During that tour, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister made a gesture on which I would like to draw your attention. Setting aside every political implication, and showing himself the great leader he is, he asked to visit the house of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the lovely and attractive village of Arthabaska. That trip delayed him much, but also impressed him to a high degree. He did not fail to show great interest in seeing the home and study of that great Canadian who was Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
I should like to thank the Prime Minister for his visit to our province and to remind him of the warm welcome which the population gave him. Needless to add, Mr. Speaker, that we should like him to come again often to keep in touch with Quebec people.
Being the representative of a rural constituency, before dealing with defence production, which is the field of my department, may I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to say a word about the problems of my constituency, whose main industry is agriculture, forestry and various other undertakings which are a secondary source of revenue.
The Address-Mr. O'Hurley
I realize that agriculture has its problems at present, but I am not of those who see only its problems.
I have the opportunity to meet quite regularly farmers and leaders of farm organizations of my constituency and of surrounding constituencies and they keep me posted on the developments in that field.
I have always watched with great interest the march of events in the field of agriculture and I must say that that very important class of our society deserves all my consideration.
In Lotbiniere as in surrounding constituencies, a problem exists now in the field of agriculture; it concerns the price maintenance in some sectors of production where there is overproduction, and in sectors where that overproduction recently increased substantially.
Why, for instance, those hog and egg surpluses? I think that they are the result of the so-called vertical integration, that is because companies have been set up and have taken up hog raising and egg production. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-ness) has stated on many occasions: "We shall guarantee each year a support price for A and B hogs up to 100 a year per farmer and for 4,000 dozens of eggs, grade A, for each producer. Statistics show that very few farmers exceed that quota and I mean real farmers who raise hogs and chickens on their own. So we shall keep a very close watch on the problems arising in every field, but our attention will bear mostly, for the time being, on those two categories we are more concerned over.
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this point to mention the recent decision taken by the government to make payments in April, for the first three months of the year, based on the statistics for the twelve months of the year ending next October 1. If the average price is 33c. a dozen throughout the year, a farmer receiving the 33c. support price for grade A large eggs in the year ending April 1st will have nothing to refund.
Mr. Speaker, a problem arises in my constituency in the field of forestry work; that industry has been very close to my heart for many years, and forestry work is quite profitable in my area. In the dead season, woodcutting is an important source of income for our farmers.
A new approach to woodcutting, involving new methods of cutting, of protecting forests
454	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. O'Hurley against fire and disease, and of clearing overage and harmful trees gives us hope of producing more abundant and better quality-timber, thus giving the farmers an important extra income on their farming operations.
You will agree that agriculture has been going through important changes in the last few years. Agriculture has changed from a manual to a mechanized activity, because in order to apply the many new agricultural methods that are needed by our farmers to meet competition and reduce their costs, they have to mechanize their farms. However, there is always the danger that our farmers will be carried away by their enthusiasm and will buy agricultural implements beyond their means. Therefore, agricultural leaders should make it a point to advise farmers to remain within the bounds of reason. If changes are being made in the field of agriculture, there must also be changes in the management and maintenance of farm wood-lots, and we are pleased to find that many of our farmers show increasing interest in forestry.
Mr. Speaker, a danger hangs today over our forest growers, especially sugar bush owners in the province of Quebec. As we all know, the maple industry is a profitable one in our province. Because I know that in recent years many of our forest species are exposed to disease, I want to warn sugar bush owners against a disease that came to notice last year and affects maple trees. To date we have lost our birches and our elms and now we have found traces of this disease on maple trees. Our farmers and sugar bush owners should know that at the first sign of this disease in our forests they should warn entomologists in order that this calamity may be checked or controlled immediately if possible.

When I first took over this Department of Defence Production, in the first intimate talk I had with the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) he confided to me his anxiety about the differences in purchases made by Canada in the United States and contracts from the United States in Canada. It was at his suggestion to see what could be done that, with my officials agreeing 100 per cent, that we started in late 1958 this production-sharing program. I wish to state at the beginning of my remarks that the officials in the depart-


ment right down the line not only worked intensely and conscientiously but I can say they were practically dedicated to making the result a good one in this production sharing with the United States.
It is now six months since I reported to the house, when my department's estimates were considered last July, on the progress of the Canada-United States production-sharing program. At that time I reported that we had obtained a framework of United States policy and regulations which was favourable to Canadian participation in United States defence production programs. The principal need for the future was to intensify our efforts in two directions: first, to make United States procurement agencies and contractors aware of the meaning of production sharing and of the capabilities of Canadian industry; and, second, to help our industry to find and exploit the new opportunities for sales in the United States.
I should like today to report to the house some of the more important actions we have taken during the past six months to meet those objectives. In addition, we have now had a full year's experience in the working of the production-sharing program and are in a better position to measure its progress. First of all, we have continued our efforts to ensure top level support for the program by the United States authorities. The matter was discussed, for example, at the meeting of the Canada-United States committee on joint defence at Camp David last November 8 and 9. I am happy to report that the United States secretaries joined willingly with Canadian ministers in reaffirming the importance of the program and the determination to give it continued active support.
In addition, since I last reported, there have been two meetings of Canadian and United States officials at the deputy minister and assistant secretary level, as well as frequent meetings of other officials of the two governments, in the course of which progress has been kept under close scrutiny and problems have been examined with complete frankness and resolved in a most co-operative spirit. On our own part there has been the build-up of effort which I promised last summer. We have acquired and are still acquiring additional officers for both our headquarters staff and our field representation in Washington and the major defence procurement and production areas in the United States. Arrangements have been further developed for the Canadian government to help in the administration of both prime and

subcontracts placed in Canada under the production-sharing program, and procedures are being improved for Canadian quality control inspection of such contracts.
A detailed index of defence commodities showing Canadian sources has been prepared and distributed very widely through our Washington office to United States government procurement agencies and defence contractors.
We are continuing our effort to encourage United States contractors to visit Canadian industries. So far at least 20 major United States contractors have made such visits on a comprehensive scale. In all, some 100 Canadian firms have been surveyed in this manner, many of them by a number of United States firms, and both my officials and the Canadian manufacturers involved have been impressed by the thoroughness and apparent sincerity of these plant visits. We have been encouraged to find that the United States prime contractors have reported in all cases a sound capability across a broad front within Canadian industry, and extremely high capabilities in special fields on the part of a number of Canadian firms. I might say that the visitors have been very forthright in their comments, and some of their critical findings have been of very great value.
We have also encouraged Canadian industry to present its case and seek out opportunities in the United States, with the result that about 115 Canadian firms visited United States government procurement agencies and major contractors during last year. In all, some 100 United States defence contractors have been visited.
I have on a number of occasions stressed the value of these face to face meetings between Canadian and United States manufacturers. They are, I feel, largely responsible for the fact that during the past year United States defence contractors sent 1,900 invitations to bid to Canadian firms, in response to which 1,400 tenders were submitted. I should add that 365 bids by Canadian firms were successful. I think this is a very encouraging proportion.
My officials will continue to work closely with Canadian manufacturers and trade associations to discover any difficulties encountered in trying to enter the United States defence market and to give what advice and assistance we can. I might mention in this connection, that I paid a visit in mid-October to British Columbia and had an opportunity, which I greatly appreciated, to meet with west coast manufacturers for a discussion of production sharing. Arrangements are now being made for similar talks and a visit to the Winnipeg area in the near future. I wish to
The Address-Mr. O'Hurley assure members of the three Atlantic provinces and Newfoundland that I have not forgotten the promise I gave them last summer to visit them.
I might mention that at the beginning of the year I wrote to several hundred Canadian firms to review for them the progress of the production-sharing program, and to ask for their comments and suggestions for the future. The replies to date have been very helpful to us in assessing the effectiveness of our efforts and, on the whole, indicated to us clearly that Canada's defence industries are taking this program seriously and are anxious to discover and exploit the opportunities which it represents. I should add that the replies have almost invariably contained the highest praise for the effort which the department has been putting forth to make the program succeed.
Members will recall that under the estimates approved last year provision was made for more tangible forms of assistance to Canadian industry seeking a share in the United States defence programs. During the past six months the government has, on a number of occasions, agreed in principle to underwrite tooling and pre-production costs in order to enable Canadian firms in special cases to bid on more equal terms against United States firms which have been able to write off such costs against previous orders. As a result of these undertakings a number of Canadian bids have been successful, involving orders with an immediate value of about S3j- million, and an even greater potential future business.
The other major fund provided last year in support of production sharing was designed to support a long term defence equipment development program aimed at maintaining scientific and technical ability in Canadian defence industry at a level which will enable it to participate effectively in future production sharing. Since last summer, discussions with the United States army and air force have produced agreed principles for the control and management of projects financed out of this fund to meet the future potential requirements of those services. A similar agreement is now being worked out with the United States navy. In Ottawa, a committee representing interested Canadian departments has been established to review development proposals and recommend selected projects to the treasury board, and to monitor the execution of approved projects. By the end of the year six projects with a total estimated cost of $5.6 million had been approved.
The results of all these efforts must, of course, be judged first and foremost by the

The Address-Mr. O'Hurley value of United States orders placed with Canadian defence industry. Since the Prime Minister spoke in this debate last Wednesday, it has been possible to arrive at some preliminary figures which will indicate the value of such orders during the full calendar year 1959. These give a total, for prime contracts and subcontracts combined, of $96.3 million.
This total includes the sum of $51 million for prime contracts and $45.3 million for subcontracts, and it is important, Mr. Speaker, for members to understand how these amounts are arrived at.
First of all, in both cases we have taken into account only those orders which have the direct effect of supporting Canadian defence production industry. We have excluded a wide range of contracts for such things as construction and maintenance, petroleum products, transportation and communication services. The United States has, of course, placed fairly substantial orders in these categories in Canada during 1959 -our preliminary estimate places their value at $25.1 million. But these are not considered, either by the American authorities or ourselves, to be relevant to the production-sharing program and have therefore been ignored in our record of results.
Second, the figures represent a total in each case of new contracts and amendments which increased commitments, less any cancellations or decreasing amendments relating to commitments which had been made during the year. They do not reflect all the decreasing amendments, to the extent that these relate to commitments made prior to the productionsharing program.
Third, both totals are based on a record of orders which are known to have been placed in Canada. I have called them preliminary estimates only because we do not yet know whether or not that record is complete. For the prime contracts, it probably is since all such contracts, with only a very few exceptions, are placed by the United States services with a crown company under my direction, the Canadian Commercial Corporation. We believe we know of all exceptions of any consequence. For the record of subcontracts, we depend upon a system of monthly reporting by about 350 Canadian industries and there may be a few orders of which we have not yet heard. However, it is unlikely that we have missed any subcontracts large enough to change the total significantly.
A number of attempts have been made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and by the press to compare the current record with that of past years. Naturally, we are also very interested in the results of

such comparisons. Unfortunately, however, we have run into a number of difficulties in pursuing this. As I have pointed out, our current records have been built up on the basis of the nature and aims of the production sharing program, and figures are not available for previous years on an exactly comparable basis.
What we have had to do, therefore, is to take our records of the United States prime contracts for past years-the figures shown in the annual reports of the Department of Defence Production-and delete all contracts in those categories which we exclude in our current reckoning:	construction, petroleum
products, general services and the like. This, as the Prime Minister explained, was the source of the figures which he gave the house last week. At that time, however, the Prime Minister was dealing only with production sharing orders for the first nine months of the year. Consequently, the amounts which he quoted for the years 1953-58 also reflected only the first nine months of each of these years.
On a full calendar year basis, the closest approximation we can get to figures comparable to our production sharing record are as follows: In 1958, $37.9 million; in 1957, $58.7 million-which included the American share, amounting to $33.1 million, of the cost of CF-100 aircraft supplied to Belgium by Canada and the United States jointly; in 1956, $20.5 million; in 1955, $28.5 million; in 1954, $19.2 million and in 1953, $47.8 million.
As is well known, the United States services placed substantial orders in Canada during the years of the Korean war. In 1952 United States contracts for Canadian defence manufactures amounted to just over $150 million. About the same amount, or slightly more, was ordered between April 1 and December 31, 1951, the earliest period covered by the records of the Department of Defence Production.
However, in view of the exceptional circumstances of those war years, when the United States were hastily rearming, it does not seem useful to attempt any comparisons with our current experience. It might also be borne in mind that Canada, too, was hastily re-arming. As a result, we placed direct defence orders in the United States during the same period amounting to $357 million, in addition to which there was massive Canadian subcontracting of defence production which is estimated to have totalled, at the very least, some $500 million. This, too, can be attributed to the unusual circumstances of the time, and any comparisons with our current spending in the United States would be pointless.

I should point out the curious fact that the 12-month figures which I have given for 1953 and 1954 are lower than the 9-month figures given by the Prime Minister for the same years. The explanation lies in the fact that during the last quarter of each of these years the value of terminations and decreasing amendments actually exceeded the value of new contracts and increasing amendments.
As I have said, these figures are not exactly comparable with those I gave for 1959, even after making the exclusions I mentioned. Some very minor differences may arise because the records of past years, as published in our reports, reflect the value of orders placed for the United States by Canadian Commercial Corporation and Defence Construction Limited. The exclusion of construction contracts, of course, eliminates the latter. In 1959, on the other hand, we have based our record on the value of orders received by Canadian Commercial Corporation from the United States rather than the corresponding orders with Canadian industry in which these subsequently resulted. The principal reason for making this change was that we wanted our records to agree, as far as possible, with those kept by the United States services. In the last analysis, of course, the value of orders received by C.C.C. from the United States is equal to the value of orders placed with Canadian industry, but in any 12-month period the two are very unlikely to be exactly the same.
A more important difference lies in the fact that the figures for 1958 and earlier do not include United States defence orders placed directly with Canadian industry, either by the American services or by their contractors in the United States. However, as I have already indicated, direct prime contracts are very rare and would have little effect on the totals. As for subcontracts, no records are available because there was no system of reporting such as we now have. We have, however, made inquiries both among the companies now reporting to us and with the Department of Trade and Commerce, and have been advised, in every case, that subcontracting of the kind with which the production sharing program is concerned was rare. This seems to be further confirmed by the fact that in 1959 virtually every subcontract reported to us by industry was directly attributable to the production sharing efforts of the two governments together with, of course, the co-operation of their respective defence industries.
Taking all these factors into account, it is our conclusion that the production sharing program is responsible for, in the first place, 79951-0-30
The Address-Mr. O'Hurley virtually all of the $45.3 million in subcontracts received in 1959. In addition, it would seem reasonable to attribute to the program at least some of the increase in prime contracts, since there are no specific contracts of an unusual nature or size, such as the 1957 joint arrangement for the provision of CF-lOO's to Belgium.
There is, in short, evidence of real progress. With only one full year behind us, there can be no let-up in our efforts-but we now have tangible grounds for optimism.
I should add that there are signs of intangible benefits too, which may in the long run outweigh in importance the defence orders which are obtained. It is becoming increasingly evident that, in effect, successful production sharing requires some fairly radical changes in deeply-rooted commercial habits and attitudes within both Canadian and United States industry. With every new order received in Canada we move another step in this direction. The Canadian manufacturer discovers that United States industry is not entirely the threat which he had regarded it as being; it is, in fact, a market of enormous potential. The United States prime contractor learns, by direct experience, that there are efficient sources of supply readily available to him in Canada. Not every Canadian firm will be successful, and not every United States firm will find Canadian sources; but every move in this direction can obviously have lasting effects going well beyond the defence programs of the two countries.
While the close integration of Canadian and United States defence programs in North America has led to the development of the production sharing programs, we have not lost sight of the close ties which bind Canada to other countries. Within NATO we are following closely the efforts of our European partners to develop common requirements and integrated production programs. On a number of occasions we have drawn attention to Canadian developments which seemed of potential value to the other members and have offered technical co-operation where it might assist their efforts. My department has also, in conjunction with the R.C.A.F. established close consultation with the German defence ministry concerning our common interests in the CF-104 and F-104G. Now that the Netherlands and, more recently, the Belgian air forces have adopted the same basic aircraft there will be new questions of common concern to be considered by the various governments. I propose, later in the session, to report on the progress of this program in all its aspects, including this matter of inter-allied co-operation.

The Address-Mr. O'Hurley
The government has been particularly encouraged by recent developments in our relations with the United Kingdom respecting defence equipment. For the first time in some years the United Kingdom government has turned to Canadian industry for defence equipment of significant value. The first sign of this revival of British purchasing came last September when a $2.6 million order for torpedoes was placed in Canada. More recently, as hon. members will have seen from press reports, the United Kingdom announced its decision to purchase Beaver aircraft from de Havilland of Canada. More and more we find among our friends in the United Kingdom a willingness to consider not only the merits of Canadian designs but the capabilities of Canadian manufacturers as well.
Needless to say these developments reinforce our own interest of long standing in the role which British industry can play in Canada's defence program. In recent months, for example, we awarded to a United Kingdom firm an important contract for the flight and tactical trainer which simulates operations of our large new transport aircraft, the CC-106, whose turbo-prop engines, I might add, are also of British manufacture. Even more recently, it was decided that the newly adopted wireless set for Canadian army vehicles, the C-42, will be purchased from the British manufacturer. We are more than ever convinced that co-operation in defence production with the United Kingdom can be of great value to both countries. Such cooperation, of course, reflects not only our traditional ties with the United Kingdom and commonwealth but also, as is true as well of our production sharing arrangements with the United States, Canada's interdependence with its partners in the Atlantic alliance.

I wonder whether the

Mr. Speaker, the perennial nightmare of unemployment looms just as big as ever here in Canada, and in my humble opinion no government, including the present Diefen-baker government, has had the courage to face up to this problem and do something tangible about it and about curing this ill that will ever haunt the people and the government of Canada, and retard progress and prosperity. This expedient of the government trying to provide, and persuading companies, industry 79951-0-30J
The Address-Mr. Tucker and private citizens to provide, employment opportunities during the winter to offset seasonal unemployment is commendable. Yet we must all agree that it is not the solution to the question and our problem. At most it is only a temporary remedy.
Has this government ever tried to analyse this problem and get at the root of the cause? If it has, then we have not been told the results of such investigations and what suggestions were adopted or what plans were made to try and kill this stigma on our natural progress. Did the government ever consider the fact that the figures quoted each year by the government at this season of the number of people in Canada out of work due to seasonal unemployment are never correct, because only the persons registered with the national unemployment service are counted, which is by far short of the total number unemployed. Again, the count by the national unemployment service includes all unemployed persons, some of whom have been unemployed for some considerable time previous to seasonal layoffs.
In the past two years we have treated this matter of unemployment in Canada too lightly and have not given it the consideration that the problem deserves, for whilst we have unemployment on a large scale we can never achieve that measure of prosperity and economy that we are striving for in this great dominion of ours so that we can have a happy and contented people.
As a government, we are bringing into Canada immigrants which in itself may be a good thing. We are sending money out of the country to help relieve distress and hunger in other countries, which again is commendable. But with regard to our own people, our own contrymen and women, what are we doing for them? We are asking industry, employers and private citizens to provide work for them to tide them over this year, last year and every year. Of course, the government does provide a little help in this respect by having some public works projects started during this season for that purpose, but this is only advancing some of the public works that would have to be done later anyway, just like a person getting a loan to tide him over difficult times. But the piper must be paid soon or later. Consequently, in the overall picture, it is not much of a help anyway because what they get now they cannot get later.
Another matter I would like to mention at this time is the rate of pay the government pays to casual help during this season of the year. I refer especially to those employed by the unemployment commission and by the post office in Newfoundland. The rate paid is $1 per hour, which is the rate paid after regular

This, I say, is not right, as according to government law and enactments, whether provincial or federal, the rate which employers are bound to pay for overtime is time and one half. Why, then, should any government take unto itself such liberties to pay just what they please, thereby profiting by the misfortune of the unfortunate people of Canada who find themselves out of work during this particular time? If employers used similar methods, what a howl the government would set up. So, to offset any such awkward position for the government, a law is passed making it obligatory for all employers to pay the prevailing rate of wages for regular hours worked, and time and one half for overtime. Why does the government not fall into line with the laws it makes for other employers?
Is this wage rate helping to relieve distress during the seasonal unemployment period? The national employment service should provide the answer. In some cases, people on claim, without working, were receiving more money per hour while unemployed than they are now receiving as casual workers with both the unemployment insurance commission and the post office. I say there is definitely something wrong, and it appears to me that the wrong is on the side of our government. If we are to be sincere and logical, we should not legislate to make other people-employers-pay wages at a rate that we, as a government, are not prepared to pay ourselves. The fault does not lie with the legislation, nor with the employer; the fault lies with this government and with this government's method of doing business. Let the government be honourable, reasonable and logical in its dealings with the people of Canada.
While I am on the subject of unemployment, I would strongly urge that as much of the public works program for Newfoundland as possible be carried out in the spring of each year rather than in the fall. Much of the work done on wharves, slipways and breakwaters in the fall has to be repaired in the spring or early summer because of damage caused by heavy seas and ice during the winter months. In addition, if the work were performed in the spring, the government would get better value for the money spent and the money obtained by fishermen for the work performed by them could be used to buy the materials necessary to prosecute the fisheries.
On a wider topic, it appears that instead of consideration being given to carrying out vital public works irrespective of where or in what province they may be required, consideration is extended to all provinces on a share basis, and even those provinces in which

all vital services and necessities are well cared for get a goodly share of the allocated expenditures at the expense of those provinces where public services and necessities are far behind what is required and what they should be if all the public services of Canada in all ten provinces are to be brought to the same standard, or something approaching this standard.
For example, Newfoundland has been a province of Canada for more than ten years, yet we still have not a standard gauge railway such as exists in the rest of Canada. Despite the promise made by the Prime Minister at St. John's in 1957 it seems that no serious consideration has been given to a change. In fact, this aspect of confederation has been entirely forgotten; perhaps the government is of the opinion that a narrow gauge railway is good enough for Newfoundland. If that is the case, and if the government of Canada has decided that the narrow gauge railway should remain, then I think it is the duty of the government to compensate Newfoundland in some way for the effects of this decision by at least completing the trans-Canada highway through Newfoundland at no cost to the province. The present attitude of the government of Canada in trying to appease the provinces by sharing public works on a per capita basis and not in accordance with requirements and necessity is simply playing politics with the lives and welfare of the Canadian people; it is not worthy of our day and age.
Some provinces have been in confederation for a great many years during which time they have built up their public services to a standard comparable to their requirements and adequate to meet the needs of the times. Other provinces which joined confederation years later have not had the same opportunities and have not had the same assistance in bringing their public services up to the standard considered to be necessary and equitable for a province of Canada. We in Newfoundland feel that after ten years in confederation public services have not advanced as far as they should and that the present government has repudiated the agreement with Newfoundland, torn up the British North America Act and failed to live up to its signed, solemn and sacred agreement with our province, as set out in the terms of union. We believe, moreover, that this government refused in particular to honour term 29 of this agreement; yet it has the effrontery to bring into this house for the consideration of hon. members a bill entitled a "bill of rights". What rights can any Canadian have or expect to have if the government of the day repudiates with impunity its scared,

sealed agreements as this present government did in respect of the province of Newfoundland?
Newfoundland is entering a critical period in her 10-year period as a province of Canada. We have in Newfoundland less than 200 miles of paved roads, whereas in New Brunswick they have approximately 3,000 miles of paved roads.
It was, indeed, a shock to the province of Newfoundland to receive early this year an official announcement of the closing down of the United States air force base near St. John's known as the Pepperrell air force base. It was chosen in 1940 as the first overseas base of the United States army and was then known as Fort Pepperrell. Many buildings have been built to fit into the everchang-ing pattern of this strategic defence base which covers about 1,600 acres, and on some of this land more than 200 buildings have been erected, worth, at today's value, more than $30 million. Approximately 1,100 Newfoundlanders were employed on this base, and the payroll amounted to $4 million annually. In addition we benefited by the sums spent by military personnel and by their purchasing of local supplies.
It has been estimated that the net decline in the distribution of money in the area as a result of the decision to close down Pepperrell will amount to more than $10 million a year. Hundreds of United States families rent houses, apartments and rooms in and around St. John's, paying very fair rentals. In addition, much employment has been given to those occupied in a wide variety of trades- plumbers, painters, electricians, garage mechanics, carpenters, labourers, waitresses, and so forth.
In the years 1955-56 at the peak of activity Pepperrell air force base had 5,779 enlisted men which included officers and 2,008 civilians. It is estimated that more than 30,000 Newfoundland girls married United States soldiers since the commencement of the base in 1940. In addition several Newfoundland children have been adopted by United States families.
The close-down of this base is serious enough for this government to consider some of our special economic problems on a national basis and I was very glad when the Prime Minister stated in this house in reply to my question on January 19th that everything possible will be done to offset unemployment resulting from the shutdown of the United States air force base in St. John's. But the people in St. John's are anxious to hear just what is going to be possible.
In a recent release it was shown that in the eastern section of Newfoundland there

4.000	unemployed on the west coast of Newfoundland, thus making a total of about

The national winter employment program has not helped to solve the unemployment in Newfoundland and something else must be substituted. There are no municipalities with the exception of St. John's and Corner Brook, in the sense that they exist on the mainland, and for most of Newfoundland there is no municipal organization in the province with power or resources to carry out the national winter employment program. The increased freight rates have driven freight costs to an all time high and help to make living for the residents of our province burdensome.
It may be asked in what way could this government further help the province of Newfoundland. There are many ways. For instance, give assistance in the building of schooners from 100 to 200 gross tons to be used in our coastal fleet which is practically a thing of the past. Newfoundland is an island and coastal boats will be needed to carry provisions and supplies to many of our outports.
Another way would be to construct dockyards which are badly needed all over Newfoundland to service ships, schooners, motor boats and longliners, especially at Harbour Grace and Clarenville. Approximately $500,000 is spent annually by Newfoundland boat owners in having their boats repaired outside Newfoundland.
Another way would be to construct more community fish stages because I am sure that those already built will prove very beneficial to the fisheries and also place more mobile bait depots in Newfoundland. Recently eight new units were sent to Newfoundland, each capable of holding 20,000 pounds of frozen bait.
A number of public wharves are still urgently needed and last year I presented the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) with a petition from Dildo in Trinity Bay, requesting that immediate action be taken to construct a public wharf and I hope that the said badly needed wharf will be constructed during this fiscal year.
The time has long passed for Newfoundland to have a freight-passenger boat, plying from St. John's to Halifax or Sydney, and it is hoped that some definite action in this direction will be soon forthcoming.

The Address-Mr. Tucker
I was glad to hear in the speech from the throne that a proposal will be placed before this house to extend the period during which payments may be made in respect of construction of the trans-Canada highway. The present contracts with all provinces expire at the end of the present year. If a new trans-Canada contract is reached it is hoped that Newfoundland will receive a better deal than the one now in force because it places a financial burden on Newfoundland that is almost three times worse than that of any other province. Estimates are that as much as $60 million will be required to complete the trans-Canada section in Newfoundland.
Since our last session of parliament we were glad to have a few brief visits from the member of the cabinet from Newfoundland (Mr. Browne) and were glad to hear that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) is to pay a visit. To all cabinet ministers I say, come early, more often, and stay longer, as a real welcome awaits you.
If there is any truth in the old proverb that what is forecast in the throne speech will show what policy the government has and what it intends to do for the betterment of the country and its people, then the only conclusion that one can draw from what this throne speech contains is that the government has no policy and is a shortsighted government.
The foremost topic that is facing all governments of all countries at the present time is the matter of defence and this government has seen fit to ignore this vital question and did not consider it important enough to include it in the throne speech.
I notice that the government is contemplating the rewriting of the Civil Service Act, and I hope their "purpose in this matter is not to prohibit civil servants looking for an increase in wages from time to time, as time and conditions demand.
In the past, good relations have existed between the government and its employees. The government has established the principle that civil servants receive salaries which bear a fair relationship to those paid under comparable conditions in Canadian industry. To this end a supposedly independent agency was to conduct an exhaustive study of comparable business salaries. The civil service commission has devoted a great deal of time, effort and money to doing just this. And what are the results? When the findings of the commission confirmed the government's policy of holding the line, its results are published and highly publicized, but when

the commission concludes that a pay boost for civil servants is long overdue, their conclusions are suppressed.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said that salary increases would seriously upset the budget. Is it up to the civil service to balance the budget? The government should do that. If the only way they can balance the budget is to refuse to pay fair wages to their employees then the government should not be in business.
I maintain that this new Civil Service Act should give the civil servants the right to a fair wage, otherwise the Prime Minister's bill of rights, that is supposed to give equal rights to all Canadians, will prove to be a farce and not worth the paper it is written on, just as this government considered term 29 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada. Let us be sincere when dealing with our own people.

Mr. Speaker, on entering this debate my first words must be an expression of congratulation to the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) and to the seconder, that gracious lady, the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Cassel-man), whose poise and the quality of her speech should stand as an example for all hon. members who follow her in this debate.
I must also congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) upon his elevation to his high position which duties I am sure he will carry out with the distinction he has shown in the house to date.
May I also offer my congratulations to the new Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) and to the new Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), as well as to the parliamentary secretaries.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, Springhill is in my constituency, and all hon. members are aware of the problems that have faced this disaster scarred town. It is with pleasure that I am able to inform this house that it is now well on the way to recovery. In saying this, I do not mean to create the impression that there is not substantial unemployment still existing; that there are not problems still to be faced; but what I do mean is that the town's survival is assured and it is my sincere hope that 1960 will see a marked change in its economy.
We saw first in Springhill, after the disaster of 1958, the location of the Springhill Woodworking plant through the work of the Nova Scotia government; then, the establishment of a battery factory, nearing completion at the present time-again with the assistance of the Nova Scotia government-and the announcement of the location of a new federal

penal institution at or near Springhill, and the still later announcement that the former mine site would be the site of this institution. I know the residents will be pleased to learn that an announcement is expected shortly on the tender award for the construction of the temporary buildings associated with the institution, and they will be further appreciative when this work is completed and inmates are moved in, which we hope will take place early this summer. Late in 1959 the spirits of the people were further lifted with the announcement of the opening of a new mine, again assisted by the provincial government.
As hon. members will note, the situation has improved considerably since I spoke last in the house and, although there is still much to be done, we in Cumberland have a great deal to be thankful for in this regard.
May I now turn to transportation, for in this field lie the hopes and fears of all in the Atlantic provinces: the hopes that we can overcome our present transportation problems, thereby bringing our area a new prosperity, the opportunity to catch up with the rest of Canada, and the fears that this will not be done or that it will not be done in the bold and imaginative manner that is necessary if we are to catch up.
This government through its many programs in the past three years has greatly assisted the Atlantic provinces; indeed, I dread to think where we would be today without the $100 million grant to the provinces, the thermal power program, the increased subventions on coal, to mention just a few; but it must not stop now, for we are on the way up. Today in the Atlantic provinces there is a new attitude replacing the old. The old was to run to the government for a loaf of bread and then accept the crumbs that were tossed from the table. Today we are aware that we have a government quite willing to give the loaf if it can be shown that the project proposed is feasible and sensible for the over-all good of the area. Today, this attitude is made abundantly clear by APEC, by the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, which has many fresh ideas on its editorial pages, and by the Atlantic Advocate, a magazine that is today without equal in promoting the welfare of the Atlantic area.
But this new approach does not stop there. It filters down to local boards of trade and individuals. Last year we learned from the premier of New Brunswick that an economic survey would be carried out by an independent group into the feasibility of the Chig-necto canal from an economic standpoint. He did not say the government at Ottawa should do it; he said we would do it ourselves, and if the report is optimistic, then we will press
The Address-Mr. Coates our case with Ottawa. This is the only sensible approach to matters of this nature and we all look forward to the results of this survey.
In my constituency, the town of Parrsboro enjoyed a ferry service across the Minas basin to the Annapolis valley for a period of 90 years until, in 1940, as a war measure, the ferry was removed. It was moved to an area where it could better serve our cause and the people accepted this inconvenience for the period until the end of the war but, as things have so often happened in the east in the past, it was the end of the service. Here was a transportation link, provided for a period of 90 years, maintained through a federal subsidy, that disappeared. In the 90 years it operated the ferry's value decreased for with the coming of the automobiles and trucks of this modern day the type of facility, old-fashioned and inadequate, did not change. This ferry service was of a tidal nature and, because of the lack of proper docking facilities, could not make scheduled runs. In 1945 there was no great hue and cry for the return of this outmoded service; but it Was not long before the residents of both Parrsboro and the Annapolis valley realized what a terrific loss this service was, especially if it were re-established on an economic basis.
With this realization, committees were formed and they took their arguments to the provincial and federal governments. With the election of the Stanfield government in Nova Scotia in 1956, one of its early acts was to appoint the Acadia University Institute to make a traffic study of this proposed service. Premier Stanfield, like Premier Flemming, is aware that facts are necessary before action can be taken. The Acadia University Institute report was favourable and called for the reestablishment of the service. During this period the federal departments of public works and transport carried out engineering surveys on the cost of piers and came up with an estimate of approximately $10 million.
The Nova Scotia government was not completely satisfied with the cost figures on the piers; they felt there must be alternative methods and had an engineering survey carried out as well. Their engineers recommend an alternate type of piers which will cost in the vicinity of $6 million. Still further, the Nova Scotia government, in order to be completely certain of the traffic possibilities, had a Toronto firm also carry out a traffic survey. Their approach differed from that of the Acadia University Institute, but the result was the same, favourable. In view of these facts and in view of the assistance such a service would provide to the agricultural industry in the Annapolis valley-always at a

The Address-Mr. Coates transportation disadvantage because of the manner in which the Minas basin cuts into the heart of Nova Scotia-to the fishing industry of the south and western shores of Nova Scotia in cutting many miles off their trips to markets, to the tourist industry which means so much to the economy of the maritime provinces, may I recommend this project to the ministers of transport and public works as a vital need in our economy.
It may be argued by some that because it is within the province of Nova Scotia it is a provincial responsibility. This is not the case. It was a service, provided through federal subsidy, taken from us by the federal government in time of war and never returned. It is necessary to the economy of the maritime provinces, and this was clearly shown by the maritime provinces' boards of trade last June when they met in Saint John, New Brunswick, and supported the re-establishment of this service. Could this project not become a part of the trans-Canada highway program? I say it could and should.
It was with a great deal of pleasure, Mr. Speaker, that I learned from the Minister of Public Works of the naming of the new headquarters building located on Riverside drive in Ottawa after Sir Charles Tupper. This recognition of Sir Charles Tupper is in keeping with the contribution he made during the conferences leading to confederation, as well as after as a member of the Macdonald cabinet and as prime minister of this country. This announcement follows closely the publicity given to the late Hon. J. Layton Ralston, another great Canadian whose birthplace was Amherst, the shiretown of my constituency. May I recommend to the minister of northern affairs the erection of a memorial in Amherst in order that attention is drawn to the fact that Amherst was the birthplace of Sir Charles Tupper, and that Cumberland was the contributor of four fathers of confederation as well as cabinet ministers to both the Conservative and Liberal parties down through the years.
When I speak of Sir Charles Tupper a matter comes to my mind which has been receiving a good deal of attention in recent days. I refer to the use of Wallace sandstone in the construction of federal buildings in the maritimes. This is not a new problem. In fact, it was one which existed when Sir Charles was the member for Cumberland and, in an effort to promote its use, he was able to have sandstone from Wallace used as one of the building materials in the original parliament buildings.
In recent days it has come to my attention that limestone from outside the maritimes would be used as the building material in a new federal building to be constructed in

Glace Bay. On learning this, I immediately communicated with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) and the Minister of Public Works. As a result of our representations the minister is obtaining an alternative quotation to ascertain the possibility of having a building material from the maritimes used in this new structure. The Halifax Chronicle-Herald had this to say about the use of a material from the maritimes in the construction of federal buldings in an editorial dated January 23, 1960:
Present plans of the Department of Public Works require the use of limestone of a type found chiefly in Quebec. There can be no quarrel with the product of another part of Canada but it appears sound to suggest that when a local resource is available it should be preferred over an import.
The bringing of stone into this province is akin to the carrying of coals to Newcastle. With a foundation of rock as varied as the successive geological periods through which it was laid down, Nova Scotia possesses this commodity in an abundant and comprehensive measure. With such a supply at hand it appears unnecessary to bring this heavy material from beyond our borders.
Nor is it easy to believe that local stone is unsuitable. Many homes and other structures have been fabricated from the substance of the earth's surface. Brick from clay, slate, ironstone, sandstone, beach boulders-these are but a few of the materials successfully used by Nova Scotia builders. If this region cannot duplicate the stone of another area, it most certainly can provide a suitable substance, one which is often superior.
From the economical point of view, sight must not be lost of the unemployment problem which confronts us. Use of a local product involves the province's working force and this, in turn, brings in the dollars needed to bolster the economy.
It is to be hoped that serious consideration will be given by Ottawa to using Nova Scotia stone or brick in the building of the post office at Glace Bay, as in all other public structures here. It would mean not only more employment, but would not the folk of the Cape Breton mining town also generate an even greater measure of pride in the new building because it was finished with a native material?
The words contained in this editorial are only too true. The Minister of Public Works is to be congratulated upon his efforts in this regard. It gives me pleasure also to report that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan) has informed me he is making every effort to see that Wallace sandstone is used in the new federal building slated for New Glasgow. The hon. member for Col-chester-Hants (Mr. Kennedy) is making a similar effort in connection with the federal building slated for Windsor. Is this not the co-operation that was promised the people of Nova Scotia by the Conservative candidates during the last election campaign?
In conclusion, I wish to bring to the attention of the house one further point concerning Wallace sandstone. Shortly after the editorial of January 23 appeared I received a letter from an eminent physicist in Nova Scotia who had been closely associated

with Wallace sandstone as a building material. He pointed out that the stone is much better in appearance than any of the imported varieties, and indicated the reason it had not received the consideration it deserves. In order to have this stone finished it is necessary to ship it to New Brunswick or Quebec because Nova Scotia is without modern facilities for finishing and cutting stone. The transportation charges involved in the finishing of the stone almost remove it from the competitive field. Let us hope this situation is rectified by the establishment of a modern cutting and finishing plant in the Wallace area.

I take my function as a member of parliament too seriously to waste my time identifying the cars owned by the hon. members in this house. I must say quite frankly that if I spent my time doing this I would certainly not be appreciated by the people of Beauce constituency. If the people of Montmagny-L'lslet are satisfied with such remarks, well it is up to them.

The speech from the throne which was presented to us was most vague and, particularly, most incomplete. I call to witness the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) himself, only a few hours after the address, chose to announce legislation which the government had not seen fit to include, or nad simply forgotten to include in the throne speech itself.
Among the few pieces of legislation it contains, we find the government's intention to create a new department, the department of lands and forests, so as to co-ordinate research and promote production and conservation of natural resources in Canada with regard to woodlands.
To date, only the provinces have such departments for administering woodlands inside their limits, and it is to be hoped that this department will be able to give significant service without raising any jurisdictional issue with the provinces.
The speech from the throne also indicates the government's intention of extending the delay which had been determined with regard to payments concerning the trans-Canada highway, a project which was to be completed by the end of 1961.
Such a decision could be most advantageous for the province of Quebec, which has not yet seen fit to join that program and which consequently has lost millions of dollars each year in the last few years.
Here, I especially call upon the associate minister of defence who, according to his November speech in Toronto, seems to be somewhat in the confidence of the present Quebec provincial government. I would ask him to press his friends to have the province participate in that program.
I should like now to make a few comments in regard to suspension of mortgage loans by the government and the nefarious results of that decision. It was the Minister of Public Works himself, in his message on the occasion of national housing week, who said that housebuilding is of vital importance for every Canadian.
The minister added, in reference to national housing week, that this was an occasion for each and every one of us to remember that home building plays an important part in Canada's economic development, and that the housing industry ranks second on the national level-immediately after public works-in the field of capital investment.
The Address-Mr. Racine
And according to a report published in Le Devoir on September 26, 1959, the minister went on to say this:
There is every indication that housebuilding will continue to spearhead our expansion in future years. As the minister responsible to parliament for the operations of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is the federal government agency in the field of housing, I am particularly concerned with the achievements of the house building industry.
Housing construction must maintain its healthy condition. With the help of each and every citizen, at all levels of society, we shall, no doubt, reach our goal.
The Minister of Public Works at that time asked in that message, the help of each and every one. And yet the government of which he is a member was the first one to withdraw when it froze mortgage loans and unexpectedly stopped them.
As recorded in a Canadian Press release dated November 5, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), when explaining the suspension of those loans, stated that new loans would have little effect. The minister at that time was speaking on a C.B.C. television program entitled: Press Conference.
The great moneyman of this government emphasized that, even if the government lent more money right now, the effect on the number of house starts this winter would be scarcely perceptible, as the season was already far advanced.
I do not at all agree with that statement, for the suspension of the loans left those who have to deal with construction or other connected industries rather in a quandary, as they were not given any assurance that the loans would be re-established in the near future.
There are, in my riding, large forest operations-
