(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I do not have here the statistical data my hon. friend is asking for. If he wants to wait until I have finished my speech, he could then make his remarks about C.M.H.C. loans.
There are in my riding extensive forest development projects that were curtailed after this government announcement. We cannot blame forest contractors for doing as they did and for not relying on the vague and inexplicable policy of the present government.

The Address-Mr. Racine
This government policy gave rise to a feeling of uncertainty in the building forecasts for 1960 and even if the Minister of Public Works stated in his October 30 announcement that he did not think the freeze on credit facilities would affect winter employment in the building industry, I do not share his opinion.
I agree that the 20,000 houses started through loans granted in August, September and October will keep on supplying employment this winter, but on the other hand, related industries have reduced their output with the result that lay-offs are taking place.
The rise of interest rates from 6 to 6| per cent is hardly more encouraging and will certainly not prompt anyone who wants to build a home to do so when money is as scarce as it is now.
In the field of labour, unemployment is still rampant and the government has no effective policy to cure this ill.
The statistics I got from the unemployment insurance office of St. Georges de Beauce show that nothing has changed in our area as far as unemployment is concerned. And according to the statistics obtained, from November 1, 1959 to December 16, 1959 inclusively, there has been a 5 per cent increase in the cost of claims, as compared to the same period last year, which is not very encouraging and should be noted by the government.
In a televised speech, the Associate Minister of National Defence said that the government had taken dynamic steps which had proved most successful. Among other things, as a solution to unemployment, the minister mentioned house building-that statement was made on October 10-while he probably did not know that the Minister of Public Works, twenty days later-that is, on October 30-would announce that C.M.H.C. loans were being suspended.
Another measure announced by the minister and which, according to his forecasts, was to improve the unemployment situation, was the so-called improvement to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not see how that could reduce unemployment, and its main purpose was, above all, to replenish the unemployment insurance fund, of course at the expense of the workers.
The minister also mentioned another measure, that is, federal assistance to municipalities for winter works. That is a measure which has not obtained the results contemplated by the government, and several

municipalities did not avail themselves of it, realizing that the federal government's offer was not even sufficient to cover the supplementary expenses involved in winter works.
Furthermore, municipalities had another problem on their hands in 1959, and that was the difficulty of obtaining funds; there again, when they did obtain funds, it was at most exorbitant interest rates, a result of the present administration.
If we take a look at the statistics of the Quebec municipal board, we readily realize that municipalities must borrow at interest rates reaching unprecedented levels.
On September 2, the city of Abord a Plouffe, in the constituency of Laval, borrowed $965,000 at a net interest rate of 7.28 per cent; once again, that is quite different from a similar issue, made at the rate of 5.59 per cent, in September 1958.
On October 27, the municipality of Ste. Brigitte de Montmorency borrowed $55,000 at a net cost of 7.65 per cent. Yet in 1955, the same municipality had floated a loan at an interest rate of 4.32 per cent.
I could go on adding to the list, which clearly shows that interest rates have increased to such an extent that they practically preclude any new works being undertaken by municipalities, except in emergency cases.
When you think that a town such as Sillery, which in March 1958 borrowed at a net cost of 4.91 per cent, had to face a rate of 6.93 per cent on October 19, 1959, I can imagine that it will limit itself to really urgent works.
With the government measure not being too attractive and with this exorbitant interest on top of it, I seriously doubt that the municipalities, however much they may wish to co-operate in relieving unemployment, are financially able to help the Conservatives solve the problem.
That is why I disagree with the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) when he looks upon the so-called help to the municipalities as an efficient legislation particularly now when money is tight, because the present government has captured the market in order to pay its deficits.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who, during the last election, promised that nobody would suffer from unemployment as long as he would be Prime Minister, might perhaps incite his government to accelerate public projects, as he promised to do.

The Address-Mr. Racine
The government could, as it indeed does, go on with projects that have already been prepared and provided for by the former government, and add to them the works it has promised to have done.
The construction of post offices, for instance, could be accelerated in order to give employment to the jobless.
At this point, I would be remiss if I did not thank the former minister of public works (Mr. Green) for carrying on with work undertaken by the former government and endowing the town of St. Georges with the proposed federal building. I also thank him for the new post office in East Broughton.
I hope that the new Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), will follow suit and may I point out to him that in some municipalities of those counties it is urgent that similar constructions be proceeded with. Even if he announced them himself, I am sure that the voters in my riding would be most satisfied, and so would I.
In Beauceville east, for instance, it seems that the revenue of the post office would justify the construction of a postal building. I humbly ask the minister to consider my request and I am convinced that the people of that community would appreciate getting a new post office as soon as possible. The policy to be followed with regard to the erection of the other post office buildings could be based on their respective revenues.
Another good way of providing employment in my constituency would be to undertake certain works along the Chaudiere river.
I am perfectly aware that the initiative for such works would have to come from the province of Quebec, but the head office in Ottawa might get in touch with its office in Quebec to consider the possibility of undertaking the works required to prevent the damage caused by floods and ice floes along that river. Such works might be started at St. Lambert and progress upstream via St. Georges. They might be restricted to the removal of islands and obstacles which hamper the flow of water and ice floes.
According to estimates by the Beauce country employment advisory committee, such works, if started soon, would provide employment for over 200 men, and the governments would be credited with cooperating in the winter employment campaign in Beauce county. A resolution to this effect has been submitted to the Minister of Public Works, and I hope he will be able to act upon it. Another matter that is close to my heart, and which I have been raising repeatedly since my election to this house,
is the extension of unemployment insurance to Canadian citizens working in the forests of Maine and New Hampshire. I shall have a further opportunity to raise this matter, because the resolution I placed on the order paper in this regard is the fourth on the list of those to be studied of this session.
The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet told us this afternoon that his constituency is bounded to the south by the state of Maine; I hope when the time comes, he will support me, in getting this resolution passed by the house, so that the people involved in this work may receive unemployment insurance benefits.
I should like to take this opportunity to offer my warm congratulations to the members of the Beauce regional employment consultative committee for the job they have done and their public-mindedness. Naturally they do not have available the same means as the government, but that question of unemployment seems to concern them more than it does the present government.
How will those restrictions and that unbearable money situation affect the fight against unemployment? In answer to that question, I shall read a resolution adopted by the Beauce regional employment consultative committee:
This committee suggests that a letter written in the following terms be sent to the federal Minister of Finance and to the member for Beauce. The Beauce regional employment consultative committee regrets that credit restrictions jeopardize the efforts being made to find work for the unemployed during the winter season.
Such is the verdict of people of all political affiliations who work generously to find a solution to the unemployment problem without the co-operation of this Conservative government.
Our money situation had other effects. Among others, according to a pamphlet issued by the Bank of Canada, Summary Statistics, the consumer or taxpayer, since he could not get any help from the banks, the normal financial organizations has applied to finance companies.
In July, 1958, again according to that pamphlet of the Bank of Canada, small loan companies had made loans available to the amount of $1,421 million and up till November of the same year the situation hardly changed since the same statistics show that the figure for November 1958 was $1,428 million. However, things have changed in 1959 and the total loans which reached $1,486 million in July 1959 increased by $68 million

The Address-Mr. Racine for five months only, and we find that the amount borrowed from those finance companies in November 1959 was $1,554,000.
Unable to borrow from regular sources, because this government monopolizes all the money available to meet its deficits,-the consumer went to those companies which lend at prohibitive interest rates.
In agriculture, a new policy has been established concerning quotas on hogs and eggs. It may be a little early to appreciate the results of this new policy. Under that program the producer will over 12 months, receive payments on 100 hogs only.
I wonder what some farmers will do who, for various reasons, were getting substantial revenue from hog breeding which they practised on a fairly large scale in order to make up for the loss of revenue on otherwise unprofitable lands.
Will this new policy mean that small local abattoirs-whose profits in many instances do not warrant the high expenses of organization for inspection and grading-will close down?
Will this new formula help solve the problem of surpluses, while maintaining satisfactory and fair prices to the farmer?
We shall probably have an answer to those questions as soon as we know the real effects of that legislation.
Without wishing to voice a final judgment on this form of farm relief, it as a (remedy for all the ills that befall the farmer. The compromise which the policy of deficiency payments represents is not a guarantee of prosperity for the farmer. The legislation rests on a principle tending to control farm production.
The farmer, who is at the same time a consumer, like all other taxpayers, has had to face a constant rise in the cost of living since 1957.
As a matter of fact, the consumer's price index shows that the cost of living index which had reached 123.1 in December 1957, had risen to a level of 127.9 in December 1959, which is an increase of 4.8 per cent.
In a branch which is of particular interest to the county of Beauce, maple products, the Stewart commission on price spreads mentioned that the price of maple syrup at the producer level is lower in Quebec than in any other province.


When one considers that Quebec, during the last ten years, produced 86 per cent of all Canadian maple syrup and 92 per cent of our maple sugar, and that the county of Beauce is the largest producer in this field, it is no wonder that I renew my request whenever I get the opportunity.
The reason given by the commission for these ridiculously low prices in Quebec is that the producer has to sell large quantities in bulk, at wholesale prices, for industrial use.
It seems to me that the government could initiate some research on the processing of this product so as to make it more profitable for the producers. The government could help the industry a great deal through research and through the giving of grants to the co-operative unions for the purchase of the necessary processing equipment.
Legislation which would be of great help to the consumer would be the reinstatement of the subsidy on sap buckets. Such legislation could be applied immediately. Every time I speak about those conditions in this house I am asked why the act that was enforced in 1940 was abandoned in 1955. I have answered many a time.
There are, at present, 21 million maple trees in Quebec and, thanks to the 1940 act, about 17 million sap buckets have been replaced. Is the former administration to be blamed for discontinuing legislation which made it possible to renew the sap-buckets when almost all of them had already been replaced? I must say that, at the present time, a great number of sap buckets should be replaced. The former administration has on three occasions taken action to help maple producers. In 1940, the preceding administration introduced the bill concerning this exchange; and the federal government undertook to pay a third of the cost of the sap bucket replacement. In 1945, the former administration passed another legislation to relieve maple sugar producers. In 1959, the government had, in fact, voted a bill to grant loans to co-operatives.
I can well remember that, last year, when I was dealing with the same matter, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), asked why the government-the former administration-had discontinued the legislation in favour of the maple sugar producers. I think that, now, like all other hon. members in the house, he will realize that, if the act was discontinued in 1955, it

is very important to enforce it again today. I also would therefore ask him to convince his Conservative colleagues before blaming the former administration for anything.
I was reading this afternoon in the debates of the House of Commons for 1950, page 3562, the words of a Conservative member who is now sitting here today. The house was then considering item 36 concerning the replacement of maple production equipment for an amount of $500,000. Here is what the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) said:
We again have this item, and I should like to ask the minister when it is going to end. An item to replace maple production equipment has appeared in the estimates in various amounts for the past fifteen years. As I said last year, if this goes on much longer we will be replacing the replacements.
I should like to point out to some hon. members of the house that it is at present necessary that those sap buckets be replaced.
I hope the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm will be able to convince them of that necessity. As the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) was saying this afternoon-and he has none the less lauded a former citizen of Mont-magny-L'Islet-that one must not forget his predecessor; I recall that, when the former minister of northern affairs and national resources-who is now the Liberal party leader in the province of Quebec- replied to the member for Wentworth who was opposing the adoption of the item because it was the province of Quebec which benefited the most from it, he said:

May I ask the hon. member for Wentworth if he is outlining the Progressive Conservative policy when he objects to this item?
And later on:

That is what you are. You object to it because it is for the province of Quebec. We know you.
I have received several requests from small companies and rural telephone co-operatives in which I was asked to support their brief to the Minister of Finance, asking an amendment to the legislation governing the industrial bank development, in order to include them.
These small independent companies provide service covering three quarters of the geographical area of Quebec and Ontario, generally outside the larger centres, where the big corporations are not interested in establishing themselves.
I hope the Minister of Finance will do something about the brief submitted to him
The Address-Mr. Racine on March 23, 1959, and to which he replied that such a request would be considered when the new legislation was introduced.
This government, which has stopped giving grants to these companies for the improvement of their equipment, could at least grant that request.
I should not like to close my few remarks without referring to the fact that the constituency of Beauce has had the great privilege of welcoming the Prime Minister of Canada during the parliamentary recess. I did not have the pleasure to shake hands with him since I seldom go to functions where I am not invited. Since there was no civic reception in his honour, I gathered that it was first and above all the Conservative party leader who had been invited. I regret that it was not the Prime Minister who was invited instead of the Conservative leader because I would no doubt have been asked to meet him as a member of Parliament for my riding and also because he could have seen by himself that the people of Beauce county can extend a warm welcome to prominent figures who honour them with their visit. And Beauce county knows how to do things properly when it is the first citizen of the country who pays them the honour of a visit. That is why I say that only Tory organizers were in charge of the visit. This explains why the Prime Minister did not get the warm reception he was entitled to expect from the honourable citizens of Beauce riding who can justly appreciate the high office of the first citizen of our country.
I do not want the Prime Minister to be mistaken and I hope that he did not take seriously the promise made by a Beauce Conservative to the effect that he would win over the riding at the next election. Being himself an expert in the matter of promises and knowing very well what he does about them, he certainly did not take his supporter's promise too seriously.
I gladly invite him however to come back in the beautiful Beauce county as Prime Minister before the next elections if he cares to come in that capacity. First of all, he could appreciate for himself the warm hospitality of the people of Beauce county and nothing could be more helpful to me in my efforts to keep the county in the Liberal fold.

(Text):
May I congratulate, and in no perfunctory way, the mover (Mr. Morissette) and the seconder (Mrs. Casselman) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, whose speeches, read together, give a very splendid report on the state of the nation. A more extensive report can be found in the report of the proceedings of this house over the last few days of this throne speech debate.
In this connection I find myself, of course, in disagreement with the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who spoke earlier today and who I regret is not in his place at this time. I recall him saying in the course of his remarks that he had found nothing in the debate so far which could be called interesting, edifying or amusing. Mr. Speaker, I for one have benefited greatly from listening to the speeches made up to this time. I think the report of this debate is a unique report of the social and political conditions in this country and of some of the problems and difficulties that confront Canadians, of the actions taken by this government and of proposals for the solution of some of the problems and difficulties to which I have referred.
You know, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Port Arthur, for whom I think most of us have considerable affection, has become a bit of an oracle in recent days. So that he will not think I have used an unparliamentary description of him, I would point out that the dictionary description of oracle is: "Any person reputed uncommonly wise and whose opinions have great weight." One can almost imagine that at a time, perhaps two or three years from now, when the hon. gentleman retires from politics, as he has said he plans to do, the hon. citizen undertaking what he might term Fisher planned parliamentary tours. I think hon. members could bring their imaginations to the point where they could see the hon. gentleman standing outside the peace tower on parliament hill, taking visitors by the hand and bringing them down the corridor here to the House of Commons and saying, "Now, my friends, we come to the place where the Canadian politicians carry on their activities". He might be expected to say, "Do not think that these activities involve any real work. Those people come down here, make speeches which they hope will sound good in their constituencies, do their best to appear as good fellows in the eyes of the prime

The Address-Mr. Stinson
minister and the other ministers and occasionally go back to the hustings and extol the virtues of their party and the government of the day". I do not think that many of us here look on our obligations in that way, nor will the visitors who might come under his direction get that impression. The hon. member was particularly critical of the role of the private member and of the level of parliamentary debate carried on by private members. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman has forgotten that in office today we have a government, and an administration, which pays very careful attention to the opinion of the private members of this House of Commons.
Very little.

I would remind the hon. gentleman and others who are interrupting at this time that the legislation which has been introduced in the last two years by this administration was introduced by people who sat here a long time as private members and who, in those many long years when they were in opposition, worked hard to bring about the ideas and legislation which are responsible for the great resurgence we have seen in recent months in the Canadian economy. It may just be, Mr. Speaker, that in the fullness of time the party to which the hon. gentleman belongs will assume political office in this country. I hope he remains in politics. I hope he stays here and listens to the debates and learns therefrom. Perhaps, when he is an old man he may be called back by his party and may some day be a minister of the crown and carry on the work which has been so well begun by this administration.
Mr. Speaker, the longer I spend in the House of Commons the greater respect I have for parliamentary institutions. I know that this respect has been deepened in recent months as a result of my having an opportunity last July to travel around a country under communist rule. In July I went by myself to the mainland of China. I went there, not merely out of a feeling of curiosity, but because I believe that in the next 50 years- and few of us will be around in public life or anywhere else when that time comes- the things that are happening in that country will greatly affect the way people will live in Canada and in all parts of the world. I went because I wanted to see how the communist political machine works and to try to determine what might be done by the government of this country and by Canadians to meet the world-wide communist offensive.
With this belief, and with these objectives, I travelled some 4,000 miles in the eastern part of the mainland. I came back detesting
the communist philosophy as I did before, but greatly disturbed by the indifference of Canadians to the communist threat and to the fact that communist controlled administrations now dominate about one third of the world's population and are steadily extending their influence. It is very difficult for a westerner to understand the attitudes and thinking habits of the present rulers of the mainland of China. I believe it is an obligation of our educators to become informed on these matters and to make the study of communist doctrine a part of the Canadian school or college curriculum.
I know, Mr. Speaker, one does not bring that kind of thing about by merely having conversations with professional educators. I intend to bring this matter to the attention of the responsible ministers in the ten provinces of Canada. This is a political philosophy, it is a way of life, which is affecting the daily conduct of millions of human beings, and yet how many Canadian can talk intelligently about the Marxist explanation of history or dialectical materialism? I suggest very few indeed. In order to defeat an enemy, we must know what he thinks; what he is trying to achieve, and the tactics he is likely to employ. The Chinese rulers, like their Russian counterparts, believe capitalism will crumble through internal weakness and the revolt of the proletariat, and will be replaced by what they term a classless society. For communists, the whole purpose of life is to promote world revolution.
When Chairman Mao or Mr. Khrushchev talk about working for peace, they are talking about peace in a world under communist domination. Education in communist doctrine is a never ending process in China today. It is carried out by a policy of mass persuasion in the kindergartens, schools, technical colleges, factories, communes, hospitals and jails. Hard work, physical and mental, is presented as the source of all wealth. In the kindergartens I saw children reading the communist version of the comic book which contrasted the greedy landlords of the past with the dedicated supervisors in the new people's communes. In a girls' school in Peking the lady principal told me that her pupils held a two-hour session each day on the subject of how they might increase agricultural production and thereby overtake what they termed the decadent bourgeois west. This was in a secondary school of 500 adolescent girls, and here they were devoting two hours a day to what was presented to them as the most pressing national problem. I wonder how many hours per year are spent by the school children of this nation on matters of that kind?

The Address-Mr. Stinson
Down the street from this school there was a huge poster depicting a Wall street capitalist shaking a bomb in the faces of eager looking Chinese workers. In the technical colleges cadres of party members conduct regular classes in doctrine and practice. These are always very closely related because there is no place in that society for the pure theorist. In 1937, Chairman Mao Tse-Tung wrote:
Marxism emphasizes the importance of theory precisely and only because it can guide action. If we have a correct theory, but merely prate about it, pigeonhole it, and do not put it into practice, then that theory, however good, has no significance.
Students at technical colleges in that country, Mr. Speaker, do not lack opportunities for practice, for each year they are sent out for two months' physical labour in the field or at dam building or on an irrigation project or something of that kind. Similar cadres are at work teaching in the factories. There the office workers are required to go down into the plant for two days each month on the machines so they will not forget that the work that really matters is done on the production line.
Near Peking I made a tour of a people's commune which was a combination of a state farm and eight agricultural collectives. Every worker was made to take part in one of the daily political discussions which were held in the mess halls after dinner. Perhaps the most politically active centres in the nation are the jails. In one jail I saw, nearly half the inmates were political prisoners. The warden told me that while it was important that a prisoner learn a trade while in jail, it was more important that he elevate what they called his political consciousness. In China today there is really no escape from the political influence. If a man seems to be wavering at all he is set upon by members of the street committee or a group of party workers who consider it their duty to reform his thinking. He is required to stand up and confess his past sins or to write out a laborious confession. If the instructor thinks it is incomplete, he is required to do it all over again.
This brainwashing, Mr. Speaker, can go on until a man begins to doubt the ordinary, simple things in which he used to believe. He gets to the point where he can hardly remember his own name. There is no place to which you can turn. If you try to find solace with your friends or children, you might find that they fear for themselves and their own future and will report you to the party.
Writers and artists are expected to express themselves in ideological terms. As


for literary criticism, a leading communist official has said that anything that is helpful to the development of productivity and social progress is good and the reverse is bad. I do not think there is anything in history as destructive of human values as this massive campaign of brainwashing. Millions of Chinese are now cut off from any connection with any ideas except those acceptable to the communist regime. Foreign books and periodicals except technical journals are not to be found in the country. The Christian ministers to whom I talked showed little interest in activities outside their country and declined to discuss social or political questions.
As the international commission of jurists reported last year, the pre-1949 judicial system has been abolished and has been replaced by people's courts. There is no written criminal code and a citizen can be arrested on mere suspicion of being a devi-ationist or, as they might call him, an enemy of the people. Civil liberties including the right to a fair trial are completely unknown in China today and hundreds of thousands of children who are receiving a good technical education have no opportunity to learn about any political system but their own. When the western democracies are mentioned, they are represented as countries ruled by greedy capitalists who control the administration of the government.
I do not presume to know how the Chinese people can be freed from the bondage of communist rule but I think that Canadians should be encouraged to go to China and to be as vigorous about defending our institutions as are the communists in extolling the virtues of theirs. I also think that the United States government must find a way of having United States correspondents and visitors admitted to mainland China. It would be useful also if students from the China mainland were invited to study in Canada. No doubt those who would come would be well indoctrinated communists, but who can assess the political effects of such students being exposed to a year or two of study in a free society?
For a long time to come the government of China will be preoccupied with the task of providing food for its rapidly expanding population. But the industrial revolution which is taking place in the country will make mainland China a major industrial power within 20 or 30 years. By that time it is to be hoped that with a rising standard of life and a closer connection with the people of India and of other countries of

the west the Chinese people will break free of the conformist communist regime which is now in control.
The question' of diplomatic recognition on the part of this government of the people's republic government has received a good deal of attention in editorial columns during the past year and has been touched upon by two or three speakers in this debate. Some observers and politicians think that public opinion is divided on this issue and that most Canadians believe that our government should extend this recognition. I do not think this is so but, in any event, I cannot see any advantage to Canada or to the free world arising from a change of Canadian policy in this regard.
This matter was discussed rather carefully by the late Mr. Sidney Smith, speaking in the House of Commons on February 26, 1959 and more recently by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) in Vancouver. I do not intend to review their arguments, but if the Chinese administration failed to meet the tests outlined by Mr. Smith a year ago they are less qualified now by reason of their excursions in the past year on the border of India.
But this is a matter, Mr. Speaker, which goes beyond questions of law and power politics. The Chinese government, the government on the mainland of China, is promoting a political ideology as part of the world offensive of the communist movement. The Canadian government should do everything in its power to resist the spread of this ideology and should give its unqualified support to the policy of the United States in this regard. When the policy of the United States is right, let us stand up and say so. There is no loss of sovereignty in staying with your friends when they are taking the right course.
How about the United Kingdom?

My friend the hon. member for Vancouver East asked the question: how about the United Kingdom? It was not long ago that I met a senior foreign service officer of the government of that country to whom I put such a question. My question was this: what advantage has accrued to your country or to the free world as a result of your recognizing that government? He said to me, "the simple answer to that question is 'no advantage' ".
I believe the course taken by the United States in this regard is right, for the following reasons. By refusing diplomatic recognition, the United States government is helping to keep alive the hopes of freedom loving people in southeast Asia. Recognition of the Chinese communist regime by the United States would be interpreted by these people as a sign that the west had abandoned southeast Asia to the communists. Diplomatic recognition would be followed by the admission of communist China to the United Nations and other world councils. This would be a great victory for Peking and the world communist movement, a victory which the west would have handed over without receiving anything in return. To those who would say that having China in the United Nations would improve the chances for peace may I point out that there is no evidence at all that the Chinese would change their anti-western policies if admitted to that body. There is overwhelming evidence that they would use their position to extend communist rule.
It is frequently argued that extending diplomatic recognition does not imply approval of the internal policies of a foreign government. I believe this is true. But I also believe that when the avowed policy of such a government is to spread the communist ideology and to extinguish free institutions- and it is just as simple as that-the government of Canada and the government of the United States should refuse recognition to the government of mainland China and attempt to take whatever political action may seem advisable in all spheres to meet the communist offensive.
I said that I have been disturbed by the indifference of Canadians to the advance of communism. 1 am equally disturbed by the complacency of Canadians toward certain trends in our own economic and political system. With the resurgence of the economies of the countries in western Europe Canadian exporters are going to find it harder to sell their goods in that market. Management and labour representatives should be working together to bring down the prices of Canadian goods. In this connection I think it would be useful if delegates of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Labour Congress-and some of those delegates are in this city today; that is to say delegates from that latter body and I have had the opportunity already today to bring this proposal to their notice-held a conference this spring which should be named "the bring down prices conference". We have had from the opposition suggestions-one as recently as today, I believe, from the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin)-that this conference should be convened by the

Perhaps each of them has come to think that the government should take the lead in a matter of this kind. I think it would be a very healthy thing if business and labour undertook projects of this kind on their own initiative and without forever leaning on the government and looking to the government for the solution of all their problems. They would be setting a very fine example to other organizations in this country.
Mr. Speaker, recently a Toronto educator said that you cannot build a strong nation out of a soft people. While there is increasing interest in public affairs, and I have evidence of this in my own constituency, I am not satisfied that our educators are making their students aware that they are going out into an increasingly tough and competitive world. I said earlier that students should be taught what the communists believe and how they operate. It is equally important that they should be taught what their responsibilities are as free citizens.
A Toronto paper reported on January 9 that in a poll of the first year class at the University of Alberta, half the students could not locate Ottawa on a topographical map of Canada. With the acquiescence of parents, students are placing athletic achievements and social standing ahead of high standing in the classroom. With this scheme of priorities, how in the world will they be able to compete with people of other countries where hard thinking and hard work are the only things that matter?
For many years in this parliament there have been debates on federal aid to education. There are bills on the order paper in respect of education, and I hope to have an opportunity to speak more fully on this subject later in the session. I am familiar with the constitutional difficulties in this regard, but I think we should remember that this constitution- by that I mean the British North America Act-was written almost one hundred years ago and that many concerns which were expressed at that time have no foundation today. I have not met one member of parliament who did not believe that we should work toward equalization of opportunity for all Canadians in the field of education. No doubt much can be done in this regard through the machinery of tax rental agreements and tax sharing arrangements; but I think that a federal advisory board on education-and I advocate the establishment of such a board-


would be of great value in the matter of curriculum and in the matter of promoting educational research.
A survey conducted last year by Anthony Frisch of Toronto, the results of which are published today and which are in the hands of hon. members, shows that there is strong support for such an agency from members of parliament, members of legislatures and chairmen of school boards across Canada. Such a board could be quite adequately financed for many, many years by a sum of money equal to the price of a single Bomarc installation.
In a recent issue of the Ottawa Journal the editor proposed some new year resolutions, one of which was as follows:
To quit viewing things with alarm but to act instead with the serenity and courage that befits representatives of so fortunate and prosperous a people.
While I have not adopted the first part of this resolution, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think that any of us can, I think that all hon. members will support the second.

The Minister of Agriculture may go on saying that the farm net revenue has increased in 1958 by 20 per cent over 1957, he may say that the Conservatives have done more in two years than the Liberals in 22 years, but he will never bring farmers to believe that they make more money. The best proof is found in official statistics. Despite the speeches of the Minister of Agriculture, the net revenue which the farmers got from the sale of farm products decreased by $181 million as compared with the last ten years of the Liberal government, that is from 1946 to 1956.
In previous debates during last session, we gave figures in this house. As soon as we gave a figure the Minister of Agriculture jumped up to say they were wrong. I challenge him to refute the value of the figures I give today because they come from official statistics.
I see that the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson), a great friend of the exminister of agriculture, Mr. Gardiner, would like to ask a question. I ask him to be good enough to wait until I am through.


That is the reason why the western farmers came to ask the Prime Minister to give them the parity prices he had promised them during the election.
If the western farmers are discontented and demoralized, eastern farmers are not less so. As a matter of fact, our farms are being abandoned. Farmers are leaving their land by the thousands, not to speak of the young people who do not want to stay on the farm any more because they have no hope to earn a living or to be able to found a family or assure their future. They are deserting the land and are swelling the ranks of the unemployed in the cities.
One of the causes of anarchy prevailing in our farm industry today, originates in the farm price stabilization act which was advocated by a Minister of Agriculture who has no experience and no overall concept of our farm economy.
Hear. Hear.
He does not know what he is talking about.

It did not take two years for that legislation, enacted on March 3, 1958, to show its worth.
After having fixed the price of certain farm products on the basis of purchase, the minister now changes his mind to adopt the deficiency payment system; a rather strange solution to a problem which the government brought about itself.
The reason for the change of approach confirms the incompetence of a government without foresight. To check hog surplus production, it penalizes those producers whom it had itself urged to produce. The only one responsible for the present situation is the government itself.
On April 1, 1958, without anyone asking for it, the Minister of Agriculture increased the floor price from $23 to $25, thus urging industrial merchants and others to raise hogs.
Something, of course, had to be done to check that surplus production or to compensate for the mistakes made by the minister, but why should the farmers and producers be paying for those mistakes?
The minister expects, with his scientific method, to penalize big producers to the advantage of little ones. He should take care not to stub his toe. He will no doubt solve the surplus problem but such a policy will not solve the case of small and middle breeders.
The Minister of Agriculture stated in a press release that from 90 to 95 per cent of

farmers would be entitled to deficiency payments; theoretically, it is true, but in practice it is quite a different story. I claim it is a mistake to assume that from 90 to 95 per cent of the producers will benefit from deficiency payments.
The breeders are not necessarily those who deliver hogs on the market.
Many of them have specialized in breeding piglets for sale to other breeders who fatten them up to 200 pounds.
On October 21 last, the Minister of Agriculture stated that, as from January 11, 1960, the government would stop buying surplus hogs at fixed price, that it would leave them on a free market, even if it meant direct deficiency payments to producers. This caused concern to breeders who had specialized in piglet breeding. Many of them became discouraged and gave up that type of breeding, after selling their piglets for as low as $5.
Now, the new support price system which was advocated to protect small producers will have helped wipe them off the market.
I should like also to say a few words about the egg price support policy. On August 26, last, the Minister of Agriculture stated that the government formula for buying eggs at 44 cents a dozen would be changed and replaced by the new system of deficiency payments, which means that the government would guarantee the difference between the average national price paid to the farmer and the guaranteed price of 33 cents for grade A large eggs, up to a maximum of 4,000 dozen, to the producers who had registered at a grading station. This legislation was enforced on the first of October of last year, despite many protests from all parts of the country.
With this new system, the minister wanted to slow down production which was constantly accumulating.
However, the responsibility for the surpluses rests with no other than the government.
Indeed, on May 5, 1958, the Minister of Agriculture increased the price of a dozen eggs from 38 to 44 cents, though no chicken breeder group had requested such action.
Can we then blame chicken breeders for organizing, so as to take advantage of those prices? Could we have blamed them for capitalizing, mechanizing and taking better care of their livestock? No.
A year later, that is on May 7, 1959, the short-sighted Minister of Agriculture made another official announcement to the effect that changes were forthcoming in the hog and egg support price system, that deficiency payments would be made on limited production.

It was then that protests were raised in the newspapers and in chicken breeders' associations. Nobody wanted those deficiency payments. Instead, the minister was advised to lower the support price, even if it meant amending the act. No attention was paid to the protests and the minister as always, imposed his arbitrary system. It has been in force now for close to four months, but the effects can already be seen.
I have here the prices now being paid to chicken breeders in western and eastern Canada. In a review published in the Montreal Gazette for Wednesday, January 27, 1960, egg prices for Regina were quoted at 12c. to 14c. for grades A and B, and pork prices at $18.20 per hundredweight.
